For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

content.content:
## 15. Decisions on record (owner, 2026-08-13, and the work-as-work review of 2026-08-15)

The eight questions this design opened, as answered, followed by the standing
entries and the 2026-08-15 review's decisions (14–21). Where an answer changed
the design rather than confirming it, the section it changed is named.

1. **Invocation is a CCR API call** (§12). Reverses per-project-scheduling
   §12.6; the session-creation credential in every repo is an accepted cost.
2. **The precondition re-runs at pickup, and forcing loses its exemption**
   (§6.4) — conditioned on preconditions asking task questions, not calendar
   ones. #515's rationale does not survive the pull model.
3. **Timing in a precondition is advisory, not forbidden** (§6.4): permitted
   where the verdict cannot flip between creation and pickup for scheduling
   reasons alone. No check — the property is not mechanically checkable, and
   the residual failure is a visible `task:obsolete`, not a wrong result.
4. **A precondition is go/no-go, never maybe-later** (§5) — *changed the
   design twice*. First cut: one verdict per occurrence at the first tick
   after the anchor, which required a `lastTick` read from the Actions ledger
   — a partial rebuild of the very watermark §1 complains about, called out
   as such when the owner asked for a state assessment. Resolved by the
   owner's **standing-item model** (decision 13 below): the verdict stays
   once-per-period, and the memory moves onto the item itself (`Not-before`
   roll), deleting the ledger read entirely. Mid-window firing stays out; a
   task wanting finer latency declares a finer `frequency`.
5. **The fleet concept is eliminated** (§12, §13) — *changed the design*.
   Wider reach is a different invocation endpoint, declared by the task that
   needs it. `ready-for-agent-fleet`, the second executor routine, and
   `session_scope` all delete. (One elaboration flagged in §12: the task names
   an endpoint *key*, with the URL and credential in repo config, so no
   vendored pack file carries deployment detail.)
6. **The executing-leash reclaim rides the tick** (§11) — *changed the
   design*. ~2h to recover a dead executor's item instead of ~25h; the janitor
   keeps the judgment sweeps. Amends the 2026-08-06 single-recovery-site split
   in siting, not in principle.
7. **Namespaced labels, executor identity in claim comments** (§4). As
   drafted; the sketch's literals and a label-per-executor are both declined —
   the first for queryability, the second because executor identities are an
   unbounded set.
8. **Dependency readiness is the tick's alone** (§9). No re-check at close: one
   site evaluates `Blocked-by`/`Not-before`, and ~1h per chain link is within
   what nightly work tolerates. *(Amended by decision 19, 2026-08-15: a second
   site at close, with the tick as backstop — the ~1h/link stacked on drain
   occupancy once the work step was priced honestly.)*

Standing entries — no decision needed now:

9. **Known limitation (S18):** a fan-in blocked on a stuck child waits for a
   human; no quorum or deadline semantics at this scale. The janitor's stale
   escalation is the visibility. Revisit only on evidence.
10. **Ref-creation CAS claims** — `refs/claudinite/claim/<n>` is the
    platform's one true first-writer-wins primitive and would replace the
    comment lease outright. Recommendation stands: keep comment leases
    (visible on the item, sufficient at this concurrency) unless a real
    lost-race incident occurs. Recorded so it is not re-derived.
11. **Invocation idempotency key** — **answered at implementation: there is
    none.** The endpoint is a routine's API trigger (`POST
    /v1/claude_code/routines/<id>/fire`), whose body accepts one freeform `text`
    field and no idempotency key. The conclusion drawn from that was initially the
    wrong one — build a lease to clean up the duplicates — and the owner corrected
    it (2026-08-15): **don't create the duplicates.** One call per item, no retry,
    the unanswered case left to the agent leash (§6.6), and §7's claim protocol
    deleted rather than written.
12. **The no-go record alternative** — every occurrence creating an item born
    closed on a no-go was recorded here as the only ledger-free way to keep
    every occurrence on record, priced at ~2,500 closed issues a year.
    **Superseded by decision 13**, which achieves both properties (no ledger,
    every ask on record) with one *rolling* item per task instead of one
    closed item per occurrence.
13. **The standing work item** (owner, 2026-08-13) — *the generation model,
    settled*. The tick creates each task's item unconditionally at its anchor
    and evaluates nothing; the precondition runs exactly once per period, at
    pick, on the executor; a no-go **rolls** the item to the task's next
    anchor instead of closing it, so the item carries "asked, declined, wakes
    at T" and the tick is a pure function of the clock and the issue list.
    Forcing a scheduled task becomes waking its standing item. One
    elaboration of the owner's literal proposal, flagged in §9: `after`
    compiles to a pick-time yield, not a `Blocked-by` edge — a rolling item
    never closes, so blocked-by would starve dependents of a quiet upstream
    forever (S24). Titles carry no timestamp; the issue number is the
    identity, as ever.

The work-as-work review (owner, 2026-08-15). The correcting premise, in the
owner's words: *"The pre work is not pre work. It's work. Sometimes there's
also agentic work. The work can take time. The work can crash. The work
creates PRs. The work is a lot."* Every sizing assumption in the design was
re-derived under it — the mechanics survived; the arithmetic and the
deployment coupling did not:

14. **The work step is the work** (§6.5) — the executor-side subprocess is the
    whole task for most of the fleet; the agent phase is the judgment
    minority. The design names the phase **the work step**; the vendored
    contract key stays spelled `code_work` until its own rename migration
    (tracked in the follow-up issue), because renaming a key every member's
    files carry is a fleet migration, not a doc edit.
15. **Heartbeat comments during the work step** (§6.5, §11) — *changed the
    design*: F17 reframed (heartbeat interval < leash replaces leash >
    every work bound), the `timeout-minutes ≤ leash` run cap retired (§6),
    and the item's timeline stays live through long work. One mechanism
    serves recovery and visibility.
16. **The tick never waits on a drain** (§10) — *changed the design*: the
    double-tick serialization scopes to the tick alone; executor work runs
    outside that concurrency group, or the heartbeat's legal long runs would
    starve the hourly tick behind the platform's queueing.
17. **The occupancy capacity model** (§10): a drain's throughput is its
    serial work-step occupancy, so `maxItems` and executor width are the
    primary capacity parameters; self-re-dispatch (`workflow_dispatch`, one
    of the two events a `GITHUB_TOKEN` can fire) is the drain-until-empty
    shape; the oldest-first fairness exposure is named and accepted at
    today's scale.
18. **The terminal comment is the durable record** (§6.5): the
    `claudinite-task-exec` record and every artifact the work created land on
    the item at close — Actions logs expire, and for agentless runs (the
    majority, under this review's premise) the item is the only durable trace.
19. **F1 reopened — readiness re-checks at close** (§9), amending decision 8
    in siting, not principle: whoever closes an item readies its dependents in
    code and a drain follows; the tick stays the backstop. (S33, S4.)
20. **Randomized pick order, adopted outright** (§6.1) — *amended 2026-08-15,
    same day*: first recorded as "ship with width", then adopted
    unconditionally on the owner's rebuttal of the one argument against —
    the stale-ready escalation is period-scale, so nothing in the system
    leans on minute-scale oldest-first ordering. Urgent first, then random
    among the ready.
21. **"Tick" keeps its name for now** — the owner's naming rule (spell names
    out; no single nouns that need contextual reading) applies to everything
    new here ("the work step", "the readiness re-check at close", "heartbeat
    comments"), and renaming the tick itself is deferred to
    [#877](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/877) so it lands
    after the old slot scheduler's vocabulary retires and the
    "scheduler"-name collision is moot.
22. **One executor run performs one item — structurally** (§6, §10) —
    *amended 2026-08-15, same day*: first recorded as "`maxItems` defaults to
    one", then the knob deleted on the owner's correction ("An executor
    performs a task. It's not a current value. It's the essence of it.").
    A run claims one item, sees it to its settle, and ends; a run ending
    with items still pickable re-dispatches a fresh run, so the queue drains
    run by run and a run's timeout sizes to a single work bound. The sim
    models runs as first-class objects with a recorded trigger on every run
    — asserted by S34. (Engine: the `maxItems` surface deletes and the
    dispatch plumbing lands via #883.)
23. **A dead executor run must not stall the re-dispatch train** (§10, §11):
    the executor workflow carries a failure-continuation job — `needs:
    execute`, `if: failure() || cancelled()`, which the platform runs on a
    fresh runner even after a timeout or runner loss — whose one step
    re-dispatches the workflow. The remaining queue resumes in ~a minute;
    the dead item itself still waits for the leash reclaim; the tick drain
    stays the backstop behind everything. (S36; wiring rides #883.)
24. **The operator hold: `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`** (§8, owner,
    2026-08-16) — cancelling one run means "move on" (intent already served
    by the continuation + leash); stopping the *system* is a repo Actions
    variable every workflow checks as its first act, exiting having fired
    nothing. Items freeze untouched; resume is clearing the variable — the
    next cron tick self-heals everything, or a hand-dispatched **scheduler**
    run (not the bare executor) does it immediately. (S37/S38; wiring rides
    #883.)
25. **`task:done` / `task:obsolete`** (owner, 2026-08-19) — the `outcome:`
    namespace dissolves into `task:`: one vocabulary carries the state
    machine's live and terminal states alike (§4). `outcome:delivered` stays a
    read-only legacy spelling — nothing writes it. The fielded engine keeps
    the old spellings until the vocabulary migration; decoders map every
    legacy spelling straight to today's, per the stored-data rename rule.
26. **The origin marker is deleted** (owner, 2026-08-19) — *changed the
    design*: standing vs ad-hoc derives from structure (§3) — an unqualified
    item of a task with a frequency at HEAD *is* the standing item; a manual
    task's item, or any qualified item, is ad-hoc; a request item is known by
    its `Request:` field. `origin:request` dies unbuilt; fielded
    `origin:schedule` labels become inert stored data the decoders ignore, and
    the vocabulary migration may strip them from open items. The one semantic
    shift, accepted: an unqualified ad-hoc twin of a scheduled task ceases to
    exist as a concept — creating one is minting/waking the standing item
    (§8's lever), and deliberate concurrency names a qualifier.

# Claudinite work-item executor (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6, §10) — a pull worker
# over the queue, triggered by a `task:ready` / `task:urgent` label event for
# latency and by hand for a drain. It carries NO cron: the tick's own drain job is
# the poll that makes a lost label event irrelevant, so events here are latency
# sugar and never the only delivery.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the tick and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A label event on anything else is not this workflow's business — and a
    # workflow_dispatch carries no label at all, so it always runs.
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # MUST stay ≤ the engine's executing leash (60m): a hung runner has to be
    # killed by the platform before its claim is reaped and the item re-picked, or
    # a zombie's code-work runs beside its replacement's (F17).
    timeout-minutes: 50
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # Hand-maintained, like the tick beside it: the canon runs its own engine
          # at the repo root and no converge writes its workflows, so this list is
          # what the stub's `# claudinite:secrets` stamp produces on a member.
          FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
          CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  # A run that dies — crash, timeout, cancellation, runner loss — never reaches
  # its own re-dispatch, so without this the queue would sit until the next cron
  # fire. The platform runs this job on a FRESH runner after any such death
  # (DESIGN §10, S36), and its one step fires that dispatch instead: the
  # remainder drains in ~a minute, while the dead run's OWN item waits for the
  # executing leash to reclaim it — nothing here touches that item.
  #
  # `continuation_depth` is the stop. A run that dies at startup — a broken
  # engine, a revoked token — dies identically every time, and an unguarded
  # continuation would dispatch itself for as long as that lasts; after three the
  # chain stops and the tick's own drain is the backstop, one hour out.
  continue-the-chain:
    needs: execute
    if: >-
      (failure() || cancelled())
      && fromJSON(inputs.continuation_depth || '0') < 3
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const depth = Number('${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}' || 0) + 1;
            const ref = context.payload.repository?.default_branch
              ?? context.ref.replace('refs/heads/', '');
            await github.rest.actions.createWorkflowDispatch({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              workflow_id: 'claudinite-executor.yml',
              ref,
              inputs: { continuation_depth: String(depth) },
            });
            core.info(`the executor run died — dispatched a fresh one on ${ref} (continuation ${depth} of 3)`);
====
# Claudinite work-item queue — the generator tick and its drain (tasks-dispatch
# DESIGN §5, §10). This is the repo's ONLY cron, and it replaces the slot
# scheduler's content at the same path when `taskScheduler.dispatch` is `"queue"`
# — same file, same hashed minute, different mechanism, so the one-cron rule and
# every reader that knows this workflow by name keep holding.
#
# A thin shim: all logic lives in the vendored engine, so this file changes
# rarely. The minute below is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge
# rewrite it to this repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50, computed by
# `node engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs <owner/repo>`.
#
# TWO JOBS, IN ORDER. The tick is pure label mechanics over the issue list —
# instantiate each task's standing item at its anchor, ready what is due, reclaim
# dead executor claims — and evaluates no precondition and collects no signal. The
# drain is an ordinary executor run: it picks up what the tick just created, which
# is what keeps the common case's latency at zero even with no `labeled` event
# delivered. Lost events are therefore never the only delivery — they are latency
# sugar, which is what retires the re-arm.
#
# `workflow_dispatch` is not a convenience: it is the never-wait-for-the-cron
# lever every forced run, migration and validation burst depends on. Its one
# input is how that lever reaches ACROSS repos: the fleet enforcer dispatches
# this workflow naming the tasks to run now, and this member wakes its own
# standing items with its own token (DESIGN §8). The alternative — the enforcer
# editing every member's issues directly — would widen the fleet PAT to issue
# writes on every repository, for a job the member can do for itself.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '44 * * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      wake:
        description: 'Task ids to run now (`pack/task` or a bare task name, space-separated) — wakes each one’s standing item regardless of its anchor'
        required: false
        type: string

# One tick at a time, always. The tick's duplicate-standing-item self-heal is
# written assuming exactly this — it closes every open family item but the oldest,
# which is safe precisely because two ticks never run at once.
concurrency:
  group: claudinite-tick
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write        # read the repo + vendored engine; a task's code_work pushes its delivery branch
  issues: write          # create / label / comment / close work items — the queue itself
  pull-requests: write   # a task's code_work opens its PR and arms auto-merge
  actions: write         # dispatch a workflow a task drives (creating a workflow_dispatch event needs write; `read` silently 403s the POST)

jobs:
  tick:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Instantiate, ready and reclaim work items
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          CLAUDINITE_WAKE: ${{ inputs.wake }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/tick.mjs

  # The post-tick drain. `timeout-minutes` MUST stay ≤ the engine's executing
  # leash (60m): a hung runner has to be killed by the platform before its claim
  # is reaped and the item re-picked, or a zombie's code-work runs beside its
  # replacement's.
  drain:
    needs: tick
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 50
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Drain the queue
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # On a member this block is stamped by the wiring converge (the
          # `# claudinite:secrets` marker in the stub); the canon has no converge,
          # so its own list is written here, by hand, in the same commit.
          FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
          CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  # A scheduled run reaches no one when it goes red, so escalate a whole-run
  # failure to a human-visible `workflow-failure` issue. Converges to ONE open
  # issue by a fixed title (create-or-comment), and ensures the label first since a
  # first-run failure may precede any label-ensure.
  report-failure:
    needs: [tick, drain]
    if: failure()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite scheduler run failed';
            await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' }).catch(() => {});
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${owner}/${repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            const body = `The Claudinite tick/drain run failed: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels: ['workflow-failure'], body });

the item already *carries* its schedule in `Not-before`, so a calendar
   precondition would be a second clock disagreeing with the first. Timing
   belongs to `frequency`, the anchors, and `Not-before`. The rule is
   **advisory** by owner ruling: no mechanical check (the property is not
   checkable), and the residual exposure is an item rolled with a calendar
   reason in its record — visible, and it costs a cycle, not correctness. The one live offender is resolved by
   ruling rather than grandfathered: **baselining's `ageDays > 1` gate is
   dropped outright** (owner, 2026-08-13: "the wrong precondition"). Its
   precondition becomes the work question alone — is the mount behind canon
   head, are migration notes unapplied — with cadence carried by
   `frequency: daily-2h` and nothing else. The corpus enters the new mechanism
   with zero calendar preconditions.
5. **The work step**, Action-side, unchanged contract: subprocess, task dir
   cwd, `required_secrets` as env, timeout, `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`
   conditional hand-off. **This step is the work, not preparation for it**
   (owner correction, 2026-08-15): for most of the fleet it is the whole task —
   long-running, crash-prone, PR-creating — and the agent phase is the
   sometimes-important judgment minority. The contract key is still spelled
   `code_work` (renaming a vendored key is a migration, tracked separately);
   the design calls the phase what it is. Three requirements, the first
   stated explicitly since SCENARIOS S8/F12:
   - **Re-entrant** — a dead executor's claim is reclaimed and the item
     re-picked, so the work can run again over its own half-done output (it
     already must survive this today, where a scheduler run dying mid-work
     leaves the slot due; the contract just never said so).
   - **Heartbeat while it runs** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the
     executor comments on the item every ~15 minutes during the work step.
     The heartbeat is what lets one short global executing leash survive
     arbitrarily long work — the leash measures executor *death* (heartbeats
     stopped), never work *duration* — and it is the item's visibility during
     the hours its timeline would otherwise go dark (§11 has the leash
     arithmetic this replaces).
   - **The terminal comment is the durable record.** Actions logs expire; the
     item is what remains. Whatever ends the item — converge here, or the
     agent later — the closing comment carries the `claudinite-task-exec`
     record and every artifact the work created (PR links above all). For an
     agentless task this comment is the *only* durable trace of the run, which
     is what makes it non-optional.

   Failure → comment + `needs-human` + a sub-label, `task:executing` removed —
   and **the worker chooses which sub-label**. The executor sees an exit code
   and nothing else, so it cannot tell a token missing a scope (a person's
   five-second fix) from an exception in the worker's own code (an afternoon);
   a worker that knows prints `claudinite-needs-human: <kind> — <detail>` on
   either stream before exiting non-zero and the park routes on it. Read from
   the output rather than a file, because it must survive the SIGKILL at
   `code_work_timeout` — output is echoed live, a file written at exit is never
   written at all. The last marker wins, so a sweep may revise its verdict as
   it works through its targets; no marker parks at `failure`, which is what
   every worker written before the marker existed does in every run.

## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism

The default deployment stays one vendored cron workflow — the repo's only
cron, rule unchanged — containing the tick job and a drain (the tick runs
first; the executor drains what it created, which keeps the common case's
latency at zero even without events). Event triggers (`task:ready` labeled)
give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup — with one platform fact
worth knowing: a label written by a workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` emits no
triggering event (GitHub's recursion guard), so events only ever come from
*foreign* tokens — a human, a CLI on a PAT, an agent session. The drain being
in-run is what makes that harmless; it is the structural delivery, events the
sugar.

**The capacity model, honestly** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the work
step is the work, so throughput is run *occupancy* — one run, one item, and
the queue drains as a chain of runs. The CCR sessions runs hand off
parallelize for free; the executor-side work does not. So executor width is
the primary capacity parameter, not a garnish: scale with a matrix width for
parallel executor jobs, or with executors outside Actions entirely — the
contract is "issue read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner
anywhere with a token qualifies. The chain itself is **self-re-dispatch**:
`workflow_dispatch` is one of the two event types a `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can*
fire, so a run that ends with ready items left re-dispatches the executor
workflow and a fresh run continues.
One fairness note, accepted at today's scale: the randomized pick (§6.1)
removes any *systematic* head domination, but a heavy item still occupies its
run for the full work bound while light tasks wait out the chain — a sentence
here rather than machinery, until it is measured.

**What starts an executor run is an enumerable list, and each cause is on the
record** (2026-08-15, and the sim asserts it — S34): (1) **the tick's own
drain job** — the guaranteed delivery, started by the cron workflow's job
graph (`needs: tick`), no event involved; (2) **a `task:ready`/`task:urgent`
label event** — foreign tokens only, the latency sugar; (3) **the close-time
drain** — whoever converges an item triggers a drain when anything is
pickable after its readiness re-check (§9); (4) **self-re-dispatch** — a run
that ends its one item with others still pickable dispatches a fresh run;
(5) **the failure continuation** — a run that dies (crash, timeout,
cancellation, runner loss) never reaches its re-dispatch, so the executor
workflow carries a second job, `needs: execute` with `if: failure() ||
cancelled()`, which the platform runs on a fresh runner and whose one step
re-dispatches — a dead run stalls the train by ~a minute, not until the next
cron fire (S36). Causes 3–5 ride `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
`GITHUB_TOKEN` *is* permitted to fire — the explicit exemption in the same
recursion guard that suppresses its label events — so no wider credential is
involved.

**The tick must never wait on a drain** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15).
The heartbeat retires the sub-hour cap on executor runs (§6), and a long
drain sharing the tick's serializing `concurrency` group would then hold the
next cron fire — instantiation, readiness and the leash reclaim all stalling
behind the very work they schedule. So the serialization the double-tick
guard needs (S6) scopes to the **tick alone**, and executor work runs outside
it: the drain leaves the cron workflow's concurrency group (its own group, or
the separate executor workflow via dispatch). A deployment where the drain
can still block the tick is mis-wired even while nothing visibly fails.

Executor identity is self-declared in claim comments; the system never
enumerates executors, which is why adding one requires telling no one.

## 11. Recovery — what the janitor keeps, what dies

| failure | today | proposed |
|---|---|---|
| scheduler/tick miss or late fire | run-ledger catch-up math | same property from the occurrence guard (§5) — the next tick instantiates the most recent occurrence only |
| double tick | concurrency group + slot-title search | concurrency group + occurrence-guard search (same window, same answer) |
| lost label event | janitor re-arm (remove/re-add), 20-min grace, bounded by stale escalation | **retired** — executors poll on the tick's cron; events are latency sugar, never the only delivery |
| duplicate events / racing executors | claim lease on one implicit executor | same lease, N executors — the loser picks a different item |
| executor died mid-claim | — (executor was a session; janitor reclaimed via `agent-running`) | **the tick** (owner, 2026-08-13): `task:executing` with no activity past ~1h → strip to `task:ready` with a comment, so a dead executor's item is back in the queue within ~2h rather than ~25h. An executor iteration is minutes, not hours, and a lease checked once a day is not a short lease |
| executor run died with items still queued | n/a (one implicit executor; the next slot was a day away) | **the failure-continuation job** (owner, 2026-08-15): `needs: execute`, `if: failure() \|\| cancelled()` re-dispatches on a fresh runner, so the *queue* resumes in ~a minute while the dead run's own item waits for the leash; the tick drain is the backstop when the whole workflow run is lost (§10, S36) |
| agent session died mid-run | janitor: stale `agent-running` → `needs-human` after ~3h | same, on `task:agent` (a hand-off comment names the session, so the janitor can say *which* session died) |
| CCR invocation lost | undetectable (label event fired into the void); surfaced only by re-arm/stale | **synchronous**: a refused call converges `needs-human` with the error at once; an unanswered call leaves the item with the agent and the agent leash settles it — one call per item, never retried (§6.6) |
| item never picked up | stale dispatch escalation, period parsed from the slot id's leading char | same escalation, period read from the task's declared `frequency` at HEAD (or a default for ad-hoc items) — no title parsing; the stale item converges `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-action` — the lane is not being drained and the fix is outside the item — and leaves the queue |
| dependency never resolves | n/a | **the stale-ready rule cannot see it** — a blocked item is never ready (F14, caught by the simulator against S18's claim). The janitor gains a third rule: a blocked item whose blockers have not resolved for ~2 days gets an escalation *comment* — labels untouched, so the item still proceeds by itself the moment its blockers resolve; a human who decides it is dead closes it by hand |

The janitor remains an ordinary daily task and shrinks twice over: re-arm and
its grace window delete, and the **executing-leash reclaim moves to the tick**
— a deterministic label rule, serialized and hourly, which is exactly the
tick's kind of work. This amends the 2026-08-06 "all recovery lives in the
janitor" split, deliberately: the split's purpose was that recovery happen
*once, in one place, in code* rather than in every triggered session, and a
rule that runs once per tick satisfies that as fully as one that runs once per
day. What stays with the janitor is everything needing judgment or a longer
horizon — four rules and a review: the dead *agent* claim (`task:agent`
silent past ~3h → `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-decision` (what the dead
session left behind decides whether this re-queues), the hand-off comment naming which session
died), the stale-ready escalation (unpicked past ~2 periods →
`needs-human`), the stuck-dependency sweep (F14 above — comment-only), the
stateless-item repair (an open work item wearing neither a `task:*` state
nor `needs-human` — a torn label swap's leavings, §6.2 → `needs-human` +
`task:needs-human-decision`),
and the health review, which gains the queue (ready-item age, blocked-item
depth, outcome mix) as its subject and can now compute all of it from
issues.

Two leash constraints, made explicit by the validation review (2026-08-13) and
the first **reframed by the work-as-work review (2026-08-15)**:

- **The executing leash measures executor death, never work duration — the
  heartbeat is what buys that (F17, reframed).** As first written, F17 made
  the leash exceed every task's work bound, which under the work-as-work model
  inflates it to the heaviest task in the fleet: one legitimate three-hour
  task and a dead executor on a two-minute task also waits three hours to
  reclaim. Instead the executor **comments a heartbeat on the item every ~15
  minutes during the work step** (§6.5): a live run is never reclaimed however
  long it works (S31c), a dead one stops heartbeating and is reclaimed within
  ~the leash of its last heartbeat regardless of the work's bound (S31d), and
  the wiring-time conformance check shrinks to the one relation the heartbeat
  itself needs — **heartbeat interval well inside the leash** (S31). The
  livelock the original constraint prevented — every tenure reclaimed alive
  before it can finish, the work re-executing forever, nothing converging —
  is still demonstrable by switching the heartbeat off (S31b), which is why
  the heartbeat is contract, not courtesy. The paired runtime rule is
  unchanged: an executor **re-verifies its own lease at every state
  transition** (is my claim still this episode's earliest?) and abandons
  silently when it is not — which is what keeps a reclaimed-but-alive runner
  from handing off work it no longer owns.
- **The agent leash (~3h) assumes agent sessions finish or touch their item
  within it** — parity with today's stale `agent-running` sweep, stated as
  an assumption rather than discovered as an incident: a legitimately
  longer-running agent must comment on its item to reset the activity
  clock, or it will be declared dead. (The same move as the executor's
  heartbeat, at the other hop.)

Both recovery sites keep the same discipline: **recovery is code, run in one
place per rule, never a sweep inside a session that is executing something.**

{"number":801,"title":"Migration to the work-item queue: two PRs, one same-day validation burst","body":"The phase plan for [tasks-dispatch DESIGN](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md) (§14 points here). Design constraints from the owner (2026-08-13): **fewest disparate steps, fewest approval points, and certainty the same day** — we do not wait for a nightly run to learn whether the end state works. Deliberately generating real work to push traffic through every path is explicitly sanctioned.

**Approval points: two.** PR‑1 (mechanism + canon flip) and PR‑2 (fleet flip + slot deletion). Everything else is forcing and observing, which the mechanism itself defines as ordinary operations.

Checkboxes track progress; each burst row's checkbox is checked only with an evidence URL appended beside it.

---

## Where this stands (2026-08-16 12:10Z)

**One member is verified end to end, agentic lane included. Twelve more are blocked on owner-only credential work.** Steps 0–2 complete. Step 3 is most of the way: the flip is merged and observed, the first member ran a real agentic item to `outcome:done`, and three defects the burst could not have caught were found and two fixed. The slot deletion still waits on the remaining members.

| | state |
|---|---|
| Canon | on the queue since #854; 12 clean scheduler runs overnight, 12 items to terminal state |
| Fleet | flipped by default in #888 (`17902b9`); **GCEC verified end to end**, 12 members still need a CCR routine (#916) |
| Slot machinery | still in the tree, deliberately — deleting it before members are verified strands them (see Step 3) |
| Design vs engine | DESIGN/sim current to §15.24 plus F24; engine at pre-review behavior — the catch-up is Step 4 (#883) |
| Open follow-ups | #916 (owner-only, blocking), #921, #892, #924, #883, #877 |

## Step 0 — rehearsal (done)

- [x] Simulator + scenario suite green in CI; coverage map names the live-only rows

## Step 1 — PR‑1 on canon: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (approval №1)

- [x] Label vocabulary, tick workflow (cron + `workflow_dispatch`), executor workflow, janitor re-target, dependency fields + `after` yield + `create-work-item`, F8 signal exclusions, canon flipped, gate green
- [x] **Approval №1: PR‑1 merged** — #854, `b30ef77`

## Step 2 — the validation burst (complete)

- [x] **B1 creation + first-item rule (S25):** [run 31899008771](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31899008771) — 12 items #860–#870, each `task:blocked` wearing its next anchor
- [x] **B2 the roll + reasons on record (S1′):** #860 — one ask, rolled to tomorrow, reason on the item, no comment spam
- [x] **B3 agentic happy path + real CCR invocation + records (S2):** #867 — wake → claim → hand-off with nonce → **live session in 31s** → result + exec record → `outcome:done`
- [x] **B4 agentless path end to end:** #859 — wake → executor in 2s → claim → prework → `outcome:done`, closed in 26s, no session
- [x] **B5 the chain + yield (S4/S23):** #863 — yielded while `core/update` was live ([run 31913047785](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31913047785)), then claimed and running the moment the upstream cleared; its work merged as #887
- [x] ~~**B6 hourly cadence**~~ — **dropped** (owner). `create-extractor` is `gcec/create-extractor` on GoogleCalendarEventCreator, the fleet's only hourly task; canon has none
- [x] ~~**B7 missing-secret posture**~~ — **folded into Step 3** (owner): every member reaches the flip with its endpoint token unset, so the posture happens on real traffic with no scaffolding
- [x] **B8 force-while-executing mutex (S15):** #871 — queued behind the executing twin, then got its own verdict on release
- [x] **B9 multi-executor lease (S7):** #873 — three overlapping executors, exactly one claim, one execution
- [x] **B10 follow-up fields (S17):** #872 — `Blocked-by` + `Not-before` created and held blocked by the tick
- [x] **B11 janitor leashes:** [run 31900490000](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31900490000) — 12 blocked/rolling items, zero escalations
- [x] **All burst rows green**

### What the burst caught that the rehearsal could not

Four defects, none of which any simulator would have produced. Three are fixed:

- **#879 → #881 (merged).** Hand-off appended a second `### Context` instead of replacing the first, splitting the item's binding scope while `instructions.md` says to read "the Context section", singular. Every unit test passed, because each tested one call. Confirmed fixed on live traffic in B5's own hand-off.
- **#882 → #885 (merged).** Queue sessions wrote `[unknown]` where the exec record's slot id used to go — `instructions.md` never said what replaces it — dropping the join from a record back to its work item.
- **The task-path guard fired correctly** on a hand-built item naming `task.mjs` instead of `task.md` (#871): refused, converged to `needs-human`, nothing run.
- **#892 (open).** The terminal convergence is agent-discretion, and **both** agentic runs got part of it wrong — #867's record field, and #863 closing with no outcome label and no exec record at all. Proposes a `converge-item.mjs` the session calls with its judged outcome.

## Step 3 — the fleet flip, then the deletion (approval №2)

**PR‑2 is two PRs, not one** (amendment, 2026-08-15). The plan said "slot machinery deleted in this same PR"; that is unsafe, and the reason is in the code:

- `updates/engine-update.mjs` **replaces the mount wholesale**, so a file canon deletes leaves every member's mount on its next converge whatever that member's config says.
- `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push — staged, and landed later by the apply stage.
- The two stubs call **different entry points**: `run.mjs` vs `queue/tick.mjs`.

So deleting slots in the flip's own release strands any member whose workflow has not yet landed. Keeping the slot code makes that window benign (`run.mjs` no-ops) and #888 makes it **loud**.

- [x] The pack update flow staged only the scheduler workflow, so `claudinite-executor.yml` reached no member — #874, `5ca4c35`
- [x] **Approval №2: the flip merged** — #888, `17902b9`. `dispatchMode` answers `queue` for an absent setting, so members flip with **no edit to any file they own**
- [x] **A member's converge observed** — GoogleCalendarEventCreator, 2026-08-16 02:00:18–02:00:25Z: both stubs call the queue entry points out of the mount, `taskScheduler` carries no `dispatch` key, mount `queue/tick.mjs` byte-identical to canon HEAD, and [15 standing items created](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/918) (GCEC #904–#918). Last slot-era item was GCEC #903 at 00:09Z
- [x] **B7 lands here** — and the fault was **not** the unset secret the plan anticipated. `resolveEndpoint` fails at the *declaration*: [GCEC #908](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/908#issuecomment-5305803329) parked `needs-human` naming `taskScheduler.endpoints`, no session started. `endpoints` was declared in exactly one repo in the fleet — this one — so the flip left **every** member's agentic lane dark
- [x] **Per-member mini-burst on the first member (B1–B4 + B7 + B3 agentic)** — GCEC: agentless lane ran clean from 02:00Z; [GCEC #908 closed `outcome:done` at 11:28:16Z](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/908) via a live session started 11:16:12Z, its work landing as GCEC #923; [GCEC #907 `core/update`](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/issues/907) closed `outcome:done` 11:49:02Z, converging the mount through the queue itself
- [ ] **The other 12 members wired and observed** — blocked on #916 (owner-only: one CCR routine + `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` per repo)
- [ ] #921 folded in — DESIGN §8's force recipe yields an item `pickOrder` can never pick
- [ ] **Then** the slot deletion PR (slots.mjs, run-ledger math, exclusive claim, re-arm, `FORCE_TASKS` path, slot-conformance checks)
- [ ] The migration reports itself through the mechanism it ships: per-member fan-out items + a fan-in item `Blocked-by` all of them (S18 live) — fan-in closed `outcome:done`

### What Step 3 caught that Step 2 could not

Three defects, each invisible to the burst for a specific reason — and the reasons are the finding:

- **#906 → #907 (merged).** `queue/instructions.md` was never in the vendor set: `computeVendorSet` drops every `engine/**/*.md` behind a two-entry operational whitelist, and #854 added a third operational doc without extending it. That file *is* the behavior of a work-item session. **Invisible because canon runs the engine from its repo root, not a mount** — so no amount of canon traffic could show it.
- **#922 → #925 (merged).** F18's episode boundary was stated semantically and implemented over only the paths that already wrote a comment; the roll and the `needs-human` park end an episode silently, leaving a claim that outranks every future claimant. The roll self-heals via the leash (canon #860 sat unrunnable 17:44Z→03:32Z); the park never does. Fixed by *striking* the claim — including on the **losing** claimant, whose claim would otherwise become the earliest of the next episode. **Invisible because the simulator modelled the rule's intent rather than its artifact**, so it was correct by construction; the sim now models the artifact and reproduces the bug without the fix.
- **#921 (open).** DESIGN §8's force recipe — strip `task:blocked`, optionally add `task:urgent` — omits `task:ready`, and `pickOrder` admits on `task:ready` alone. A forced item is invisible to every executor and the run logs `nothing ready to pick up`, which looks exactly like a healthy run. **Invisible because no executable artifact pins DESIGN's prose recipes.**

## Step 4 — the work-as-work engine catch-up (#883; starts only after Step 3's verification)

#884 (merged 2026-08-16, `4380639`) changed the design under the shipped mechanism — decisions §15.14–24. **The behavior-by-behavior checklist lives in #883** — one box per capability, each stating what breaks while it's off; this plan owns only the sequencing:

- [ ] **Step 4 waits for Step 3's per-member verification** — the flip wave must be observed on the engine it shipped, not one changing underneath it
- [ ] Each #883 behavior lands burst-style per this plan's own discipline: a forced run observed on canon the same day; the workflow-touching pieces (heartbeat, decoupling, continuation job, suspend-all) additionally observed on one member's converge before the fleet's
- [ ] #892's `converge-item.mjs` is the natural carrier for #883's durable-record box — land them together, not twice
- [ ] #924 (a losing claimant's comment defers the leash reclaim) rides #883's heartbeat, which introduces the per-holder liveness signal it needs
- [ ] #877 (the tick rename) unblocks when this step closes — last, so the rename never churns files mid-migration

## Done means

- [x] All Step‑2 rows have evidence URLs on this issue
- [x] The first member flipped, wired and observed end to end — agentless and agentic
- [ ] All members flipped and observed; fan-in item closed `outcome:done`
- [ ] Slot machinery gone from the tree
- [ ] Step 4: the fielded engine matches DESIGN §15.14–24 — #883 closed
- [ ] 48h of ordinary operation as *confirmation* — explicitly not the proof; the burst was the proof

Every workflow half was **generated, not hand-written** — the output of running each repo's own vendored `converge-wiring.mjs`, landed via PR because `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push. Each diff was exactly two added lines.

## Two things this surfaced

- **Not every parked item was parked for this.** Items were re-queued only where the task is *agentic*; agentless ones (Sheepdog #213 `fleet-add-missing-packs`, EdFringeNow #379 `edfringe/refresh-tickets`) parked for unrelated reasons and were left alone, as were slot-era `[claudinite-task]` items.

## Not needed after all

The follow-up proposed here — landing the stored prompt as a tracked file so 13 routines get created identically — is moot now that the routines exist. Worth doing only if the fleet gains members later; #801 does not depend on it.

{"number":892,"title":"The queue's terminal convergence is agent-discretion, and both live runs got part of it wrong","body":"Two agentic runs have now executed on the work-item queue (#801 burst). **Neither converged its item correctly**, in different ways:

| item | task | what it did | what was wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| [#867](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/867) | `tidy-repo/tidy-issues` | closed, `outcome:done`, `task:agent` dropped, exec record printed | the record's occurrence field said `[unknown]` (#882, fixed in #885) |
| [#863](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/863) | `grow_with_claudinite/growth-extract` | closed as completed, thorough result comment, `verify-outcome.mjs` run | **no `outcome:` label at all**, `task:agent` still on the closed item, and **no `claudinite-task-exec` record whatsoever** |

The #863 session did the *hard* parts impeccably — it opened and merged its PR inside the `merged-pr` ceiling, deduped against 585 lines of existing pack prose, ran the prose-to-checks upgrade pass, verified with `verify-outcome.mjs`, posted to its tracker, and even caught and fixed a false-positive check on its own commit message. It then fumbled the bookkeeping, which is the part that is not judgment at all.

That is the shape of the problem: **the terminal transition is mechanical, and we are asking an agent to perform it from prose.** `instructions.md` step 5 is a table of labels plus "then print the `claudinite-task-exec` record" — five ordered side effects (comment, swap label, add outcome, print record, close) that a session performs by hand at the end of a long run, when its context is fullest and the remaining work looks like formality.

What it costs:

- **The outcome census is unreliable.** Outcome labels are the cross-check on exec records; an item closed with neither is invisible to both.
- **A closed item wearing `task:agent`** reads as live to anything scanning labels, and is a lie the janitor cannot correct — its sweeps are over *open* items.
- Both failures are silent. Nothing fails, nothing is red, and the item looks finished.

### Proposed fix

Give the session a deterministic converge step to call, the way `verify-outcome.mjs` already exists beside it for the ceiling check:

```
node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue  --outcome done|delivered|needs-human --summary 
```

The **agent supplies the judgment** — which outcome, and the prose of what happened. The **code performs the transition**: post the comment, swap `task:agent` off, add the outcome label, print the exec record with the item number in it, close with the right `state_reason`. Same split as everywhere else in this engine (`executor.mjs`: "the pure decisions live at the top… the shell below is the I/O"), and the executor already has all five operations written for the paths it converges itself.

`instructions.md` step 5 then becomes one command instead of a five-step checklist, and a session that stops early leaves an item that is *visibly* unconverged rather than one that looks done and isn't.

Worth doing before the fleet flip's per-member burst multiplies the number of sessions performing this by hand.

{"number":921,"title":"DESIGN §8's force recipe produces an item no executor will ever pick","body":"Found by following the documented recipe on live traffic (#801 Step 3, GCEC #907).

§8 says:

> **Forcing a scheduled task is waking its standing item** … force = strip `task:blocked`, clear `Not-before`, optionally add `task:urgent`

Followed literally, that leaves an item carrying neither `task:blocked` nor `task:ready`. `pickOrder` filters on `hasLabel(i, READY)` ([`queue/executor.mjs:58`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs#L58)) — `task:urgent` only affects the **sort**, never admission. So the forced item is invisible to every executor, and the tick will not rescue it either: its ready job transitions `task:blocked → task:ready`, and the item no longer carries `task:blocked`.

Observed exactly that on GoogleCalendarEventCreator: forced `core/update` (#907) at 11:11Z, the `task:urgent` label event fired the executor within seconds, and [the run](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/actions/runs/31943656688) logged `- nothing ready to pick up` and exited clean. A silent no-op that looks exactly like a healthy run — the failure mode §8 is otherwise careful about ("a force that finds no work *says so* where the operator will read it"). Here it says nothing to the item at all.

The engine's own re-queue instruction has it right — *"remove `needs-human`, add `task:ready`"* ([`executor.mjs:326`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs#L326)) — so this is a prose defect, not a code one. §8 frames force and the §4 human re-queue as "the same operation on the same object", which is true, and then spells only one of them correctly.

**Fix:** §8's recipe becomes *strip `task:blocked`, add `task:ready`, clear `Not-before`, optionally add `task:urgent`*, matching §4. Worth checking whether the simulator has a scenario for forcing a blocked standing item, since S-coverage would have caught the divergence if the recipe were pinned anywhere executable.

Small enough to fold into the next #801 change rather than carry alone.

{"number":924,"title":"A losing claimant's own comment bumps updated_at, so contention postpones the leash reclaim it depends on","body":"Split out of #922 at the owner's direction — a latent issue the strike does **not** fix.

The tick's executing-leash reclaim keys on the item's activity clock, which is GitHub's `updated_at`. Every claim attempt posts a comment, and a comment bumps `updated_at` — including the attempt of an executor that goes on to *lose* the arbitration and walk away.

So on an item nobody is actually working, each losing claimant resets the clock the reclaim is counting down. The busier the queue, the more executors arrive, the further the recovery is pushed out. Under a `labeled`-event executor plus an hourly drain, an item can be re-touched often enough that the leash never elapses.

This is what made the observed stall on canon #860 ~10h rather than the ~1h the leash nominally promises: the failed claims kept the item looking alive.

#922 removes the *cause* of those repeated losing claims, so the common case goes away with it. What stays is the general property: whenever an executor genuinely dies mid-claim, any later claim attempt on that item defers its recovery. Contention postpones the mechanism that exists precisely to recover from failure.

Worth considering:
- read the last **heartbeat/claim by the current holder** as the activity clock, rather than the item's `updated_at` — the heartbeat work in #883 already introduces a per-holder liveness signal, which is the natural carrier;
- or have a losing claimant not write to the item at all, which needs a claim protocol that reads before it writes (a bigger change, and it trades away the property that makes the current one correct under a stale snapshot).

Not urgent — the failure needs a dead executor *and* ongoing contention on the same item — but it should not be discovered a second time from a stall.

{"number":1089,"title":"Executor: one run performs one item, and chains the rest","body":"The first slice of #883's engine catch-up: the run-shape decisions (DESIGN §15.20, §15.22, §15.23), which are what the executor's own `for` loop contradicted.

## What changes

**`maxItems` deletes.** `DEFAULT_MAX_ITEMS`, `CLAUDINITE_MAX_ITEMS` and the loop in `runExecutor` are gone. A run claims one item, sees it to its settle, and ends — structural, not a number to raise (§15.22: *"An executor performs a task. It's not a current value. It's the essence of it."*).

**The chain replaces the loop.** A run that settled its item re-reads the queue and, if anything is still pickable, `workflow_dispatch`es the executor workflow — the exemption in the same recursion guard that suppresses `GITHUB_TOKEN` label events, so no wider credential. A run that settled *nothing* dispatches nothing: re-dispatching after a lost race argues with the executor that won, and after a claim revert it is two executors dispatching each other.

**The workflow gains a failure-continuation job** (§15.23): `needs: execute`, `if: failure() || cancelled()`, one step that re-dispatches from a fresh runner, so a run that dies before reaching its own dispatch stalls the queue by ~a minute rather than an hour. It carries a `continuation_depth` input capped at 3 — a run that dies *at startup* dies identically every time, and an unguarded continuation would dispatch itself for as long as that lasts. Beyond three, the tick's own drain is the backstop.

**Pick order randomizes** (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the ready. With one item per run, a deterministic order lets one unlucky head dominate a whole chain.

## Not in this PR

The rest of #883 — heartbeat, the `timeout-minutes ≤ leash` retirement, tick/drain decoupling, the durable record, the readiness re-check at close, the operator hold, the `prework` rename. Boxes and sequencing are on #883.

## Verification

- Full suite: 2268 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking (64 advisory, all pre-existing in packs this PR doesn't touch).
- See-it-fail: the four new run-shape tests were run against the pre-change engine (`git checkout HEAD^ -- executor.mjs`) and fail there; the two pick-order property tests fail against the old oldest-first comparator.
- Not yet observed on a live run — #801's Step 4 discipline asks for a forced run on canon the same day, and the continuation job additionally on one member's converge. That is the next step, not something this diff can claim.

- (b) DESIGN §6.5 ("comments on the item every ~15 minutes during the work step") and §11 (leash "reclaimed within ~the leash of its last heartbeat"; check shrinks to "heartbeat interval well inside the leash"), decision §15.15. Sim: S31/S31b/S31c/S31d (`scenarios.test.mjs:877–934`; S31c asserts a heartbeat every 15m of a 130m run).
- (c) Depends on nothing; everything else in the timeout family depends on it. Mostly engine (code-work-run + tick) + a new check; #801 Step 4 additionally wants it observed on one member. **It is also the designated carrier for #924**: the design's §11 wording ("of its last heartbeat") implies the reclaim clock must become the *current holder's* last heartbeat/claim, not `updated_at` — merely adding comments while keeping the `updated_at` clock leaves #924's deferral bug in place (and every heartbeat would *extend* other items' nothing, but a loser's claim comment still resets the clock).

- (a) Both comments still present: `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml:44-46` ("MUST stay ≤ the engine's executing leash (60m)", `timeout-minutes: 50`), `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml:66-73` (drain job, same), and the same text in `engine/scheduler/stubs/claudinite-executor.yml` / `stubs/claudinite-tick.yml:66-73`, plus `leases.mjs:7-10` ("The vendored workflows carry the fourth agreement").
- (b) §15.15 / §6.5; the run-cap arithmetic in §11.
- (c) Depends on box 1. Touches all four workflow files + both stubs — member workflow copies can't be pushed by the converge (staged, landed via PR), so this needs the wiring-delivery path and a member observed.
- (d) **The body's sizing formula is stale**: "size run timeouts to `maxItems` × the largest work bound" contradicts §15.22, which deleted `maxItems` and says "a run's timeout sizes to a single work bound". The correct target is one work bound + margin.

**3. Tick/drain decoupling — NOT STARTED.**

- (b) §15.16 / §10: "the serialization … scopes to the tick alone … the drain leaves the cron workflow's concurrency group (its own group, or the separate executor workflow via dispatch). A deployment where the drain can still block the tick is mis-wired even while nothing visibly fails." No dedicated sim scenario (F19 is prose); S34's trigger `tick-drain` still assumes a post-tick drain exists.
- (c) Workflow-file change (canon + stub → member delivery). Becomes *load-bearing* only when box 2 removes the 50m cap; today the cap masks it (the body says exactly this). Cheapest shape now on the table: since #1089 gave the executor workflow a dispatchable entry, the drain job could become one `dispatchWorkflow` call of `claudinite-executor.yml` — worth deciding before writing a second concurrency group.

**4. Self-re-dispatch — DONE in this branch.**
- (a) `engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:218-226`: after the one settle, re-read `pickOrder(listOpenWorkItems…)`, and `redispatch()` if non-empty, with the failure logged and the tick named as backstop; wired in `main()` at `executor.mjs:529` via `dispatchWorkflow(gh, repo, EXECUTOR_WORKFLOW_FILE, defaultBranch)`; `dispatchWorkflow` is status-checked (`engine/scheduler/github.mjs:100-…`, returns `{ok, status}` — conforms to the "read its status" rule). A run that settled nothing (lost race, revert) deliberately dispatches nothing (comment at `executor.mjs:151-157`) — consistent with S34, which requires triggers only on runs that had work.
- (b) §15.17/§15.22, §10 cause (4); S34 (`scenarios.test.mjs:643-680`) — asserts `settled <= 1` per run and trigger `re-dispatch` present.
- (c) Engine + the executor workflow's `workflow_dispatch` (already present pre-branch). Delivered to members with the engine converge *except* the workflow half (continuation input) which needs the staged workflow path.
- (d) Nothing moot. Note the design's cause (2), label events, only fire from foreign tokens — unchanged.

**Plus (comments): maxItems deletion — DONE in this branch.** No `DEFAULT_MAX_ITEMS`/`CLAUDINITE_MAX_ITEMS` anywhere in the tree (repo-wide grep: only DESIGN/sim/RULES history mentions); the loop is gone — `runExecutor` (`executor.mjs:160-228`) claims one candidate (`pickOrder(...)[0]`), settles it, ends. Header comment now argues *for* the shape (`executor.mjs:144-149`). Old tests rewritten (`engine-tests/scheduler/queue/executor-loop.test.mjs`, `executor-rules.test.mjs` in the diffstat).

**Plus: randomized pick order — DONE in this branch.** `pickOrder` (`executor.mjs:54-76`): urgent first, then a per-item pre-drawn random tie-break (`draw` map, one draw per item — correctly avoiding an inconsistent comparator), injectable `random` for tests. Matches §15.20/§6.1. Skip rules (same-title mutex, `after` yield) retained.

**Plus: failure-continuation job — DONE in this branch, with one undocumented addition.** `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml:66-97` and the stub: `continue-the-chain`, `needs: execute`, `if: (failure() || cancelled()) && fromJSON(inputs.continuation_depth || '0') < 3`, one `github-script` step re-dispatching with `continuation_depth+1`. Matches §15.23 / §10 cause (5) / S36 (`scenarios.test.mjs:681-717`) — except the **depth cap of 3 and the `continuation_depth` input exist in no design decision and no sim scenario** (your 08-20 comment discloses this). S37 (`scenarios.test.mjs:718-751`) additionally asserts the *janitor* parks — the janitor runs as a queue task through the executor, so gating the executor covers it, but the comment's phrasing "scheduler + executor" and the sim's "tick, executor, janitor" should be reconciled when it lands.

**5. Durable record — NOT STARTED (one fragment present).**
- (a) The executor's `close()` (`executor.mjs:487-493`) posts a terminal comment that carries the delivered-artifact links for the agentless path (`executor.mjs:352-357`, "Code-work did this run's work and left: …"), so the *artifact-links* half exists for code-work closes. But no close path — executor or agent — writes the `claudinite-task-exec` record to the item: the record machinery lives in `engine/scheduler/record-exec.mjs`/`run-record.mjs` and prints to the Actions log / session transcript only, exactly what §15.18 says expires. `queue/instructions.md` still has the agent print the record, not comment it.
- (b) §15.18, §6.5 third bullet ("the closing comment carries the `claudinite-task-exec` record and every artifact"). No dedicated sim scenario pins the comment's content.
- (c) **#801 Step 4 explicitly sequences this with #892's `converge-item.mjs` ("land them together, not twice")** — #892 is open, labeled quick-win, and is the natural carrier for the agent-side half; the executor-side half is a `close()`/`converge()` edit. Engine + vendored instructions only; no member workflow.
- (d) Vocabulary note: decision §15.25 (08-19, landed as #1067) renamed `outcome:*` → `task:done`/`task:obsolete`; the record-in-comment work should be written against the new vocabulary — #892's body still speaks `outcome:done` (historical, fine).

**6. Readiness re-check at close (F1) — PARTIALLY PRESENT, the smaller half.**
- (a) What #1089 added is the *drain* half on the executor's own paths: after any settle, the run re-reads the queue and dispatches (`executor.mjs:216-226` — comment even notes "this item's convergence may have readied a dependent"). But nothing *readies* dependents: no close path evaluates `Blocked-by`/`Not-before` of other items (readiness transitions exist only in the tick's job 2, `tick.mjs:~162,366`), so a dependent still `task:blocked` at close time is invisible to the re-read `pickOrder` and waits for the tick. The agent close path (`queue/instructions.md`) has neither the readying nor a drain trigger.
- (b) §15.19 (amending decision 8 "in siting, not principle"): "whoever closes an item readies its dependents in code and a drain follows; the tick stays the backstop". Sim: S33 (`scenarios.test.mjs:614-642` — fan-in readies within minutes of last blocker closing; hand-close excluded, tick backstop per S18) and S4.
- (c) Engine + instructions/converge-item (natural to land with box 5 / #892 so the agent path gets it in code). No member workflow.

**7. `prework` key rename — EFFECTIVELY DONE / the box is STALE.**
- (a) The key `prework` no longer exists as the contract spelling: #1013 (`cae5273`, 2026-08-18, on main) renamed the phase to code-work. `engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs:31-34` normalizes both legacy spellings straight to today's (`agent_preprocessing→code_work`, `prework→code_work` — single-pass, per the stored-data rename rule), `prework-run.mjs` is a compat shim to `code-work-run.mjs`, the run-record parser normalizes all three historical wire words (`run-record.mjs`), and the `task-declaration-shape` check (`packs/claudinite-growth/task-declaration-shape.mjs:75`) drives member-local cleanup. That *is* the "fleet migration with a compatibility window per the updates/* skew rules" the box asks for — no migration record was needed because normalization + the check are the carrier.
- (b) **But the box's target and the design disagree.** The box says rename to "the design's 'work step' vocabulary". DESIGN §6.5 and §15.14 as they now stand say the opposite: "The contract key is still spelled `code_work` (renaming a vendored key is a migration, tracked separately); the design calls the phase what it is" — i.e. "work step" is prose-only and `code_work` is the settled key (line 1103: "the work step (contract key `code_work`)"). §15.14's "until its own rename migration (tracked in the follow-up issue)" leaves it formally open whether a further `code_work`→work-step rename is ever intended, and this box is the only place that could mean. **This box needs an owner ruling: either tick it as satisfied by #1013 (key = `code_work`, per §15.14), or restate it as `code_work`→`work_step` — the current text names a key that no longer exists.**

## Contradictions and stale statements found

1. **The blocking rationale on #883 is stale — the most consequential finding.** The 08-19 tidy comment ("12 of 13 fleet members still unwired, slot deletion pending") and your own 08-20 comment ("Step 3's per-member verification, which waits on #916 (owner-only)") both post-date the facts: #916 closed **2026-08-16 12:32Z** with all members wired; #801's 08-17 comment checks "the other members wired and observed — all converged and verified" and "#921 folded in"; the slot deletion landed as #993 (`6bf4af0`, on main — `run.mjs`/`slots.mjs` are now shims per #1006). What remains open on #801 Step 3 is only the fan-in reporting item and #950-era confirmation, not member verification. #883's `blocked` label and both comments' stated reason no longer hold; Step 4 is unblocked on #801's own terms (including the workflow-touching boxes, whose stated gate was that same verification).
2. **Body box 2's timeout formula** ("`maxItems` × the largest work bound") contradicts §15.22 (knob deleted; "a run's timeout sizes to a single work bound"). Superseded same-day, never edited back into the body.
3. **The first #883 comment (id 5304690136) cites "S34/S35" — S35 does not exist.** No S35 anywhere in `scenarios.test.mjs`; the superseding comment correctly cites S34/S36. Anyone following the first comment's sim reference chases a phantom. (The comment's maxItems half is explicitly superseded; its two riders — serial-per-settle, and `workflow_dispatch` under `GITHUB_TOKEN` — survive and are implemented.)
4. **Box 1's wording vs the engine's reclaim clock vs #924**: the box says the reclaim "measures heartbeat silence"; the tree measures `updated_at` silence (`tick.mjs:200`), which any comment — including a *losing* claimant's — resets (#924, open, labeled blocked, riding this box per #801). The heartbeat box is only done when the reclaim clock reads the current holder's last heartbeat/claim; adding comments alone satisfies the box's letter and neither the design's §11 wording nor #924.
5. **`continuation_depth` cap of 3**: in the workflow and stub, in no design decision and no sim scenario (disclosed in your comment; §15.23's only stated backstop is the tick drain). Design/sim should either adopt or reject it.
6. **Box 7** (see above): names a key (`prework`) that stopped existing on 08-18 and a target vocabulary ("work step") §15.14 explicitly declined for the key.
7. Minor: §15.24's comment says "scheduler + executor" workflows check the hold; S37 asserts tick/executor/janitor skips — consistent only because the janitor rides the executor; worth one sentence when it lands.

## Related issues, one line each

- **#801** — open; Steps 0–3 complete in substance (slot deletion landed via #993 despite the body's unchecked box; body last updated 08-17); Step 4 = #883, its gate satisfied.
- **#916** — **closed** 08-16 (all routines + tokens wired); stops being a valid blocker citation.
- **#921** — **closed** 08-17 via #936 (force recipe fixed); #883's newest comment doesn't cite it, fine.
- **#892** — open, quick-win; designated carrier of box 5's agent half; land with box 5/6.
- **#924** — open, blocked-on-heartbeat by design; box 1 must change the reclaim clock to actually close it.
- **#877** — open, blocked; unblocks "when Step 4 closes" per #801 — i.e., last, after all of the above; the slot-vocabulary collision argument is already moot (#993), so only the churn argument still holds.

#1089 (merged) → box 5+6 together with #892's `converge-item.mjs` (engine-only, no member wiring) → box 1 heartbeat + the F17 wiring check + #924's clock fix (engine + check) → boxes 2+3 + operator hold (the workflow-file wave, one staged delivery to members, observed on one member per #801's discipline) → tick box 7 per the owner's ruling → #877.
