input.body:
Audited every box against the tree and the design before continuing. **The block is stale, and two boxes describe a world that no longer exists.**

## The block does not hold

The 08-19 tidy verdict ("blocked by #801 … 12 of 13 fleet members still unwired, slot deletion pending") and my own comment above both restate a gate that had already cleared:

- **#916 closed 2026-08-16 12:32Z** — all ten adopted members have a routine, a token and a merged wiring PR; the two dormant repos are parked by design. It was cited as blocking three days after it closed.
- **The slot deletion landed** as #993 (`6bf4af0`), with the fielded import shims following in #1006 (`c23f46a`).
- **#921 closed** 08-17 via #936.

What is still open on #801 Step 3 is the fan-in reporting item, not member verification. Step 4's own stated gate — "the flip wave must be observed on the engine it shipped" — is satisfied. Removing the `blocked` label.

## Corrections to the checklist

- **Box 2's sizing formula is superseded.** It says "size run timeouts to `maxItems` × the largest work bound"; §15.22 deleted `maxItems` the same day and says a run's timeout sizes to **a single work bound**. Read it that way.
- **Box 7 names a key that no longer exists.** `prework` was renamed in #1013 (`cae5273`, 08-18): `task-contract.mjs:31-34` maps every legacy spelling straight to `code_work` in one pass, `prework-run.mjs` is a shim, the run-record parser normalizes all three wire words, and `task-declaration-shape` drives member-local cleanup — which is exactly the compatibility-window migration this box asked for. The box's stated *target*, "the design's work step vocabulary", is also not what the design wants: §6.5 and §15.14 settled that the phase is called the work step in prose while **the contract key stays `code_work`**. Treating this box as satisfied by #1013 unless you say otherwise.
- **The first comment above cites "S34/S35" — there is no S35** in `sim/scenarios.test.mjs`. The superseding comment's S34/S36 are the real ones.
- **Box 1 is done only when the reclaim clock changes.** The box says the leash reclaim "measures heartbeat silence"; `tick.mjs:200` measures `updated_at` silence, which *any* comment resets — including a losing claimant's, which is #924. Adding heartbeat comments while leaving that clock satisfies the box's letter, neither §11's wording nor #924. The two land together.
- **`continuation_depth` (#1089) is in no decision and no scenario.** Flagging again so it is adopted or rejected deliberately rather than drifting: S36 never exercises a run that dies identically every time.

## Status

| box | state |
|---|---|
| maxItems deletion (§15.22) | done — #1089 |
| self-re-dispatch (§10 cause 4) | done — #1089 |
| randomized pick order (§15.20) | done — #1089 |
| failure-continuation job (§15.23) | done — #1089 |
| durable record (§15.18) | not started — lands with #892's `converge-item.mjs`, per #801 Step 4 |
| readiness re-check at close (§15.19) | half present — #1089 added the *drain* after a settle; nothing readies dependents yet |
| heartbeat (§15.15) + #924 | not started |
| `timeout-minutes ≤ leash` retirement | not started — waits on the heartbeat |
| tick/drain decoupling (§15.16) | not started — masked today by the 50m cap |
| operator hold (§15.24) | not started |
| `prework` rename | satisfied by #1013, pending your ruling above |

Continuing in that order.

{"number":892,"title":"The queue's terminal convergence is agent-discretion, and both live runs got part of it wrong","body":"Two agentic runs have now executed on the work-item queue (#801 burst). **Neither converged its item correctly**, in different ways:

| item | task | what it did | what was wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| [#867](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/867) | `tidy-repo/tidy-issues` | closed, `outcome:done`, `task:agent` dropped, exec record printed | the record's occurrence field said `[unknown]` (#882, fixed in #885) |
| [#863](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/863) | `grow_with_claudinite/growth-extract` | closed as completed, thorough result comment, `verify-outcome.mjs` run | **no `outcome:` label at all**, `task:agent` still on the closed item, and **no `claudinite-task-exec` record whatsoever** |

The #863 session did the *hard* parts impeccably — it opened and merged its PR inside the `merged-pr` ceiling, deduped against 585 lines of existing pack prose, ran the prose-to-checks upgrade pass, verified with `verify-outcome.mjs`, posted to its tracker, and even caught and fixed a false-positive check on its own commit message. It then fumbled the bookkeeping, which is the part that is not judgment at all.

That is the shape of the problem: **the terminal transition is mechanical, and we are asking an agent to perform it from prose.** `instructions.md` step 5 is a table of labels plus "then print the `claudinite-task-exec` record" — five ordered side effects (comment, swap label, add outcome, print record, close) that a session performs by hand at the end of a long run, when its context is fullest and the remaining work looks like formality.

What it costs:

- **The outcome census is unreliable.** Outcome labels are the cross-check on exec records; an item closed with neither is invisible to both.
- **A closed item wearing `task:agent`** reads as live to anything scanning labels, and is a lie the janitor cannot correct — its sweeps are over *open* items.
- Both failures are silent. Nothing fails, nothing is red, and the item looks finished.

### Proposed fix

Give the session a deterministic converge step to call, the way `verify-outcome.mjs` already exists beside it for the ceiling check:

```
node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue  --outcome done|delivered|needs-human --summary 
```

The **agent supplies the judgment** — which outcome, and the prose of what happened. The **code performs the transition**: post the comment, swap `task:agent` off, add the outcome label, print the exec record with the item number in it, close with the right `state_reason`. Same split as everywhere else in this engine (`executor.mjs`: "the pure decisions live at the top… the shell below is the I/O"), and the executor already has all five operations written for the paths it converges itself.

`instructions.md` step 5 then becomes one command instead of a five-step checklist, and a session that stops early leaves an item that is *visibly* unconverged rather than one that looks done and isn't.

Worth doing before the fleet flip's per-member burst multiplies the number of sessions performing this by hand.

@@ -0,0 +1,35 @@
+// THE OPERATOR HOLD (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §8, decision §15.24). One repository
+// Actions variable stops the whole queue: every Claudinite workflow stamps it
+// into its env, and every engine entry point checks it as its FIRST act — before
+// any read, like the dormancy gate beside it — and exits cleanly having fired
+// nothing.
+//
+// Why a variable rather than a commit: cancelling one run means "move on", an
+// intent the failure continuation and the leash already serve. Stopping the
+// SYSTEM is a different intent, and the only lever that existed for it was
+// dormancy, which needs a commit and a converge to take effect and another to
+// undo. A variable takes effect on the next run and clears the same way.
+//
+// What it freezes: STARTS, not running work. A run already past this gate
+// finishes its item — killing live work would leave exactly the half-done state
+// the leash exists to recover — so an in-flight run may close an item after the
+// hold goes on. Nothing NEW is ever picked.
+//
+// Resume needs no code: clear the variable and the next tick reclaims, readies and
+// drains on its own. The impatient path is dispatching the SCHEDULER workflow, not
+// the bare executor — the tick is what re-derives the world.
+
+export const SUSPEND_ALL_VAR = 'CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL';
+
+// Deliberately narrow: a variable somebody set to `false` or `0` to mean "off"
+// must not read as on. Anything else — unset, empty, a word — is not a hold.
+export const isSuspended = (env = process.env) =>
+  ['true', '1', 'yes'].includes(String(env[SUSPEND_ALL_VAR] ?? '').trim().toLowerCase());
+
+// The one line every entry point prints when it parks, so a run that did nothing
+// says WHY it did nothing — a silent clean exit is indistinguishable from a run
+// that found no work.
+export const suspendedNotice = () =>
+  `- ${SUSPEND_ALL_VAR} is set: the queue is held. Nothing is picked up, created, readied or reclaimed.\n`
+  + '  Clear the variable in repo settings (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables) to resume;'
+  + ' the next scheduled tick recovers everything on its own.';

import pathlib, re

DRAIN_OLD_CANON = """  # The post-tick drain. `timeout-minutes` MUST stay ≤ the engine's executing
  # leash (60m): a hung runner has to be killed by the platform before its claim
  # is reaped and the item re-picked, or a zombie's code-work runs beside its
  # replacement's.
  drain:
    needs: tick
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 50
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Drain the queue
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
"""

DRAIN_NEW = """  # THE POST-TICK DRAIN, DISPATCHED RATHER THAN RUN HERE (DESIGN §10, §15.16).
  # The tick's concurrency group serializes ticks — its duplicate-item self-heal
  # depends on that — and a drain running inside the group would make every hour's
  # tick queue behind the previous hour's work. Since the heartbeat made long work
  # legal, that is no longer a theoretical wait. So the drain is a `workflow_dispatch`
  # of the executor workflow: it starts in its own group, on its own runner, and
  # this job's success means "the drain was started", never "the drain finished".
  #
  # This is still the guaranteed delivery. A label event may be lost; this fires
  # every hour whatever happens.
  drain:
    needs: tick
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            await github.rest.actions.createWorkflowDispatch({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              workflow_id: 'claudinite-executor.yml',
              ref: context.payload.repository?.default_branch
                ?? context.ref.replace('refs/heads/', ''),
            });
            core.info('dispatched the executor to drain whatever this tick created');
"""

for path, entry in [('.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml', 'node engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs'),
                    ('engine/scheduler/stubs/claudinite-tick.yml', 'node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs')]:
    p = pathlib.Path(path)
    s = p.read_text()
    # cut the old drain job wholesale: from its comment block through its run line
    start = s.index('  # The post-tick drain.')
    end = s.index(entry) + len(entry) + 1
    s = s[:start] + DRAIN_NEW + s[end:]

    s = s.replace("""          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

cd /home/user/Claudinite; git add -A && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

Refs #883, Refs #924
EOF
)" && git push -q && git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD | cat

input.title: The work-as-work engine catch-up: every #883 box but the one that needs your ruling
input.body:
Closes the gap #883 has tracked since 2026-08-15: the design was reviewed and amended, the simulator followed, and `engine/scheduler/queue/` kept implementing the pre-review contract. The executor's own `for` loop — the thing that started this — was one symptom of eight.

**#883's block was stale and is removed.** It cited #801 Step 3 waiting on #916; #916 closed 2026-08-16 with every member wired, the slot deletion landed as #993, and #921 closed via #936. Step 4's own gate — "the flip wave observed on the engine it shipped" — was satisfied three days before the block was restated.

## The boxes

| box | what changed |
|---|---|
| **`maxItems` deletes** (§15.22) | a run claims one item, settles it, ends. The knob and the loop are gone |
| **Self-re-dispatch** (§10) | a run that settled its item dispatches the next; one that settled nothing does not — that would argue with the executor that won the race, or dispatch over an item it just reverted |
| **Failure continuation** (§15.23) | `needs: execute`, `if: failure() \|\| cancelled()`, capped at three, then escalates |
| **Randomized pick order** (§15.20) | urgent first, then random. With one item per run, a fixed order lets one head dominate a chain |
| **Durable record** (§15.18) | the terminal comment carries the `claudinite-task-exec` line — for an agentless run the item is the only trace that outlives the Actions log |
| **Readiness re-check at close** (§15.19) | whoever closes an item readies the dependents it held, sharing the tick's own predicate rather than restating it |
| **Heartbeat** (§15.15) | the executor beats on its item every 15 minutes while the work step runs |
| **Reclaim clock** (#924) | silence is now the *holder's*, not the issue's — a struck claim is not a sign of life |
| **`timeout-minutes ≤ leash` retired** | a run is bounded by one work step; what is left is a wedged-runner backstop |
| **Tick/drain decoupling** (§15.16) | the drain dispatches the executor rather than being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group |
| **Operator hold** (§15.24) | one repo variable, stamped into all four workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points |
| **`converge-item.mjs`** (#892) | the session supplies the judgment, the code performs the five side effects |

**`prework` → work step (box 7) is the one I did not do**, because it asks for something that no longer exists and a target the design declined: #1013 renamed the key to `code_work` on 08-18 with a single-pass legacy map, and §6.5/§15.14 say the phase is called the work step in prose while the key stays `code_work`. Treating it as satisfied — say the word if you meant a further `code_work` → `work_step` rename and I'll do it as its own migration.

## Two things I decided rather than asked

- **`continuation_depth`, capped at 3**, is in no decision and no scenario. Without it a run that dies at startup dispatches itself forever. Recorded in §10 as engine-side and dated, not folded into your §15 decisions.
- **A park that is not a failure carries no record.** The vocabulary's `success` means "ran to completion and closed"; `failed` means the run broke. An approval park — succeeded, left a PR — is neither, and a fifth status is stored data every decoder in the fleet would have to learn. Absence is the honest answer.

## Verification

- Suite: 2307 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_work` clean, `check_the_world` 0 blocking (64 advisory, all pre-existing).
- See-it-fail on every new assertion: the run-shape and record/release tests against the pre-change engine, and four targeted mutations of `converge-item.mjs` (drop the `task:agent` removal, drop the record, no-op the release, write to the request on failure) each caught by exactly the test that claims it.
- `consumer-safe-change` fired on the tick stub and is answered with a **rehearsal fixture**, not a migration record: `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push, so a record could not move members any faster than the staged PR already does. The new `old-workflows` shape carries the pre-change tick beside a current mount and proves that window is harmless.
- **Not yet observed on a live run.** #801 Step 4 asks for a forced run on canon the same day, and the workflow-touching pieces on one member's converge before the fleet's. That is the next step and this diff cannot claim it.

## Folders touched

- **`engine/scheduler/queue/`** — `executor.mjs` (one item, the chain, the record, the beat); new `readiness.mjs`, `heartbeat.mjs`, `suspend.mjs`, `converge-item.mjs`; `tick.mjs` (holder-silence reclaim, shared predicate, hold gate); `instructions.md` (step 6 becomes one command).
- **`engine/scheduler/`** — `github.mjs`: `dispatchWorkflow`, status-checked; `converge-wiring.mjs`: secret stamping is marker-only; `signals/gh.mjs`: the executor workflow's name.
- **`engine/scheduler/stubs/` + `.github/workflows/`** — the drain dispatches, the hold is stamped, the run cap retires, the continuation escalates. Both copies diffed against each other.
- **`vendoring/rehearsal/`** — the `old-workflows` consumer shape.
- **`docs/tasks-dispatch/`** — §10 describes the dispatching drain and the capped continuation.

Refs #883, Refs #892, Refs #924

That second half is **#924**: any comment moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring. A struck claim is not a sign of life.
- [x] **Retire `timeout-minutes ≤ leash`** — both workflows. Read the box's sizing formula as "one work bound", per §15.22; `maxItems` had already been deleted when the box was written. Two stale rationales went with it rather than being left standing: `leases.mjs`'s fourth agreement, and `code-work-run.mjs`'s claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it.
- [x] **Tick/drain decoupling** — the drain dispatches the executor workflow instead of being one. A second effect worth naming: it therefore runs no task code, so the tick stub's `# claudinite:secrets` marker goes, and `withDeclaredSecrets` stamps at the marker or not at all. Its old fallback — stamp under the first `GITHUB_TOKEN` line — would have put every task secret into the one job §14 says must never hold one.
- [x] **Self-re-dispatch**
- [x] **Durable record** — landed with #892's `converge-item.mjs`, as #801 Step 4 asked. One deviation, deliberate: a park that is not a failure carries **no** record. `success` means "ran to completion and closed", `failed` means the run broke, and an approval park is neither; a fifth status is stored data every decoder in the fleet must learn.
- [x] **Readiness re-check at close** — sharing the tick's own predicate, so the hourly pass and the close-time release cannot disagree about what "due" means.
- [ ] **`prework` rename** — **needs your ruling.** #1013 (`cae5273`, 08-18) already renamed the key to `code_work` with a single-pass legacy map, a shim, a normalizing record parser and a member-facing check — the compatibility-window migration this box asked for. Its stated *target* ("the design's work step vocabulary") is what §6.5/§15.14 declined for the key: the phase is the work step in prose, the contract key stays `code_work`. Tick it as satisfied, or say you want `code_work` → `work_step` and I'll do it as its own migration.

**The wiring-conformance line** ("heartbeat interval < executing leash, beside the existing wiring checks") is a **test**, not a check, and that is a deviation I want visible rather than buried: both values are engine constants shipped in the same mount, so a repo-scanning check would assert what the engine already guarantees — the shape `packs/README.md` and the local rules reject. What a member CAN drift on was the `timeout-minutes` ≤ leash relation, and that relation is what this change retires. The invariant is asserted in `engine-tests/scheduler/queue/suspend.test.mjs`, alongside the producer/consumer agreement for the hold — a knob stamped into no workflow, or read by no entry point, being the failure this repo has paid for twice (#974).

**`continuation_depth` is adopted, not silently kept.** Recorded in DESIGN §10 as engine-side and dated 2026-08-20, outside your §15 decisions, with the reason: a run that dies at startup dies identically every time. At the cap the chain escalates to the workflow-failure issue rather than going quiet.

What is left before this closes: a forced run observed on canon, and the workflow-touching pieces observed on one member's converge — #801 Step 4's own discipline, which a diff cannot satisfy.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

input.title: Every executor run logs `could not reconcile label "claude-automerge": 404`
input.body:
Every executor run on canon prints this before doing anything:

```
! could not reconcile label "claude-automerge": 404
```

Seen on `main`'s run [32368276774](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32368276774/job/96422660810) and on a branch run of #1089 at the same minute, so it is **not** from that PR — it is standing behavior on every run, and has been long enough that nobody reads the line any more.

`ensureLabels(gh, repo, [...QUEUE_LABELS, ...REQUEST_LABELS])` is the caller; `AUTOMERGE_LABEL` (`claude-automerge`) is in `REQUEST_LABELS`. The reconcile is fail-soft, which is why the run stays green — but the label is the asker's merge authorization (`MERGE_IF_NARROW`), read from a write-gated label at adoption. A label that cannot be reconciled is one that may not exist in the picker for a person to apply, which would make that authorization unreachable rather than merely unstamped.

Worth establishing before deciding the fix:

- whether the label exists on the repo at all, or the 404 is the *update* path failing on a label that does exist,
- whether the same line appears on members (it would be the same code, so probably),
- whether anything has ever successfully read `claude-automerge` off an issue here.

Filed rather than fixed in #1089 because it is unrelated to that diff, and a fail-soft warning nobody has acted on is exactly the kind that earns its own change.

---

A forced run happened and both workflows are green — but I have to be precise about what that did and didn't prove, because it changes whether "ok" is met.

**Observed live on branch code** ([scheduler run](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32368227608), [executor run](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32368280876)):
- The tick ran green and its `wake` readied [#1036](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1036).
- **The tick/drain decoupling worked end-to-end** — the branch drain job dispatched a *separate* executor run instead of running one inside the tick's concurrency group. That's §15.16 proven on real traffic.
- The new executor workflow ran green with its `continuation_depth` input, the retired run cap, and `continue-the-chain` correctly **skipped** on success.
- The engine booted with `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL` stamped and empty, read the queue, and exited clean.

**Not observed:** the one-item settle, the exec record on an item, the close-time release, and the self-re-dispatch. `main`'s executor — dispatched by my own branch drain — claimed #1036 three seconds earlier and rolled it with the old engine. That race exists *only* because branch and `main` are different code; after merge it cannot happen.

I also filed [#1096](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1096): every executor run, on `main` too, logs `could not reconcile label "claude-automerge": 404`. Pre-existing, not from this PR.

name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

* Executor: one run performs one item, and chains the rest

DESIGN §15.22 settled this on 2026-08-15 — "An executor performs a task.
It's not a current value. It's the essence of it." — and the engine kept
the pre-review loop. The `maxItems` surface deletes: a run claims one item,
sees it to its settle, and ends.

What carries the queue instead is the chain (§10): a run that settled its
item re-dispatches the executor workflow when anything is still pickable,
and the workflow gains a failure-continuation job so a run that DIES before
reaching that dispatch stalls the queue by a minute rather than an hour.

Pick order randomizes with it (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the
ready, so no unlucky head dominates a chain of one-item runs.

Refs #883

* Pin the executor's run shape: one item, a random head, a checked dispatch

The tests that pinned the pre-review contract went with it — `the loop stops
at maxItems` asserted the thing that is no longer true. What replaces it
asserts the structure: three pickable items of DIFFERENT titles (so the
same-title mutex is not what stops the run) and one settled; a chain that
continues only after a settle, and stands down after a lost race; and the
dispatch judged by status, since a 403 returns a body that reads fine.

Pick order gets a property test rather than a fixed order — a pinned order
would pass against a comparator that never shuffles.

Refs #883

* The terminal transition is code, and a close releases what it held

Two boxes of the work-as-work catch-up, which share a moment: the instant an
item closes.

The durable record (§15.18): the terminal comment now carries the
claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate
is shared with the tick's own job 2 rather than restated.

And converge-item.mjs (#892): a session ends by supplying the judgment —
which outcome, and the prose — while the code performs the five ordered side
effects. Both live agentic runs got part of that transition wrong from
prose, silently and differently.

Refs #883, Refs #892

* Pin the executor's own record and release paths (Refs #883)

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

Refs #883, Refs #924

* Design: the drain dispatches, and a dead chain escalates (Refs #883)

* Queue labels: task:done/task:obsolete, and the origin marker retired

DESIGN §15.25/§15.26 renamed the terminal labels and deleted the origin
marker; the fielded engine still wrote the old vocabulary. This is the
engine-side half.

The terminals are `task:done` and `task:obsolete`, one namespace with the
state labels. Labels are stored data on closed issues fleet-wide, so the
read side accepts every retired spelling and maps it STRAIGHT to today's
in one pass: `terminalOfLabels` is the one decoder, and the old constants
stay exported so a fielded pack that imports them still loads.

Standing versus ad-hoc is now derived rather than marked: the standing
item is the one titled with the task and nothing else, whose task is on a
calendar; a `manual` task's item and every qualified one are ad-hoc. The
occurrence guard, the dedupe, the `after` yield and the roll-vs-close
decision all read that instead of `origin:schedule`, which is no longer
written or ensured — only tolerated on items an older engine filed.

One behaviour follows from the derivation: an unqualified hand-created
item for a scheduled task WOULD be that task's standing item, so
`create-work-item` refuses it and names the two levers that do what the
operator meant (`--wake`, `--qualifier`).

The dashboard reads terminals through the engine decoder, and folds a
cached summary's legacy KEYS the same way — otherwise those rows land on
a key nothing initialised.

Refs #1064

* Ad-hoc requests: a marked issue becomes an ordinary queue run

Mark an issue `claude-task` and the next tick queues a run for it. The mode
is dispatched by the same tick, claimed under the same lease, judged by a
precondition at the same single evaluation site, handed off by the same
at-most-once call and parked in the same triage lanes — deliberately not a
second mechanism beside the queue.

waiting, a parked one is superseded.

request is an ordinary run rather than an item shape every downstream guard
has to except. It declares no code-work at all: the authorization a worker

nobody with push access asked for — push read from the permission API, not
from the payload's association, which is broader than the ask — and refuses

fails the run into the failure lane, open and re-queueable, because a
decline's write-back cannot reach an issue it cannot read.

argument, and `{ error }` joins go/no-go as the verdict a precondition
gives when it cannot answer. `model_from_request` is fenced to the built-in
task, which no pack can be.

* Request mode: the design's amendment, the built-in id, and the vendor set

Three loose ends of the same change.

The design says the precondition reads the permission API; what it actually
reads is a `request` SIGNAL that made those reads — because a precondition
is pure over collected signals, and handing every pack's precondition a
GitHub client to give this one task two reads would widen far more than the
gate it guards. §16.4 says so, and says which half still holds the verdict.

The built-in task spells its own id literally: the declaration-shape check
parses task.mjs statically and cannot resolve the constant beside it. The
two are pinned together from the test.

And the engine's blanket "an engine .md is maintainer reference" vendor rule
was dropping the built-in task's task.md — a mount whose request session has
nothing to read. Whitelisted by pattern rather than by name, since the next
built-in task would otherwise be dropped silently, and the regression test
now WALKS the queue engine instead of listing its top level, which is what
let this through.

Refs #1010

* Rebase onto the terminal decoder main already landed

#1068 landed `outcomeOf` in the queue's own module — every spelling to a
canonical word, decoded in one place — which is the read half this branch
had written for itself. Its decoder is deleted in favour of that one, and
the dashboard sweep with it: main's already reads both vocabularies.

What is left here is the half nothing else did: the engine WRITES the
current spellings, the origin marker is neither written nor ensured, and
standing-versus-ad-hoc is derived from the item and the declaration.

Refs #1064

* Rebase onto #1071 and bump the growth pack for the contract prose

{"total_count":7,"workflow_runs":[{"id":32368766036,"name":"Claudinite scheduler","display_title":"Claudinite scheduler","workflow_id":320696051,"run_number":403,"run_attempt":1,"event":"workflow_dispatch","status":"in_progress","head_branch":"main","head_sha":"208a0a5a705e8252b98e0de4f9892a7c1a01501c","head_commit":{"message":"The work-as-work engine catch-up: every #883 box (#1089)

* Executor: one run performs one item, and chains the rest

DESIGN §15.22 settled this on 2026-08-15 — "An executor performs a task.
It's not a current value. It's the essence of it." — and the engine kept
the pre-review loop. The `maxItems` surface deletes: a run claims one item,
sees it to its settle, and ends.

What carries the queue instead is the chain (§10): a run that settled its
item re-dispatches the executor workflow when anything is still pickable,
and the workflow gains a failure-continuation job so a run that DIES before
reaching that dispatch stalls the queue by a minute rather than an hour.

Pick order randomizes with it (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the
ready, so no unlucky head dominates a chain of one-item runs.

Refs #883

* Pin the executor's run shape: one item, a random head, a checked dispatch

The tests that pinned the pre-review contract went with it — `the loop stops
at maxItems` asserted the thing that is no longer true. What replaces it
asserts the structure: three pickable items of DIFFERENT titles (so the
same-title mutex is not what stops the run) and one settled; a chain that
continues only after a settle, and stands down after a lost race; and the
dispatch judged by status, since a 403 returns a body that reads fine.

Pick order gets a property test rather than a fixed order — a pinned order
would pass against a comparator that never shuffles.

Refs #883

* The terminal transition is code, and a close releases what it held

Two boxes of the work-as-work catch-up, which share a moment: the instant an
item closes.

The durable record (§15.18): the terminal comment now carries the
claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate
is shared with the tick's own job 2 rather than restated.

And converge-item.mjs (#892): a session ends by supplying the judgment —
which outcome, and the prose — while the code performs the five ordered side
effects. Both live agentic runs got part of that transition wrong from
prose, silently and differently.

Refs #883, Refs #892

* Pin the executor's own record and release paths (Refs #883)

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

Refs #883, Refs #924

* Design: the drain dispatches, and a dead chain escalates (Refs #883)

* Queue labels: task:done/task:obsolete, and the origin marker retired

DESIGN §15.25/§15.26 renamed the terminal labels and deleted the origin
marker; the fielded engine still wrote the old vocabulary. This is the
engine-side half.

The terminals are `task:done` and `task:obsolete`, one namespace with the
state labels. Labels are stored data on closed issues fleet-wide, so the
read side accepts every retired spelling and maps it STRAIGHT to today's
in one pass: `terminalOfLabels` is the one decoder, and the old constants
stay exported so a fielded pack that imports them still loads.

Standing versus ad-hoc is now derived rather than marked: the standing
item is the one titled with the task and nothing else, whose task is on a
calendar; a `manual` task's item and every qualified one are ad-hoc. The
occurrence guard, the dedupe, the `after` yield and the roll-vs-close
decision all read that instead of `origin:schedule`, which is no longer
written or ensured — only tolerated on items an older engine filed.

One behaviour follows from the derivation: an unqualified hand-created
item for a scheduled task WOULD be that task's standing item, so
`create-work-item` refuses it and names the two levers that do what the
operator meant (`--wake`, `--qualifier`).

The dashboard reads terminals through the engine decoder, and folds a
cached summary's legacy KEYS the same way — otherwise those rows land on
a key nothing initialised.

Refs #1064

* Ad-hoc requests: a marked issue becomes an ordinary queue run

Mark an issue `claude-task` and the next tick queues a run for it. The mode
is dispatched by the same tick, claimed under the same lease, judged by a
precondition at the same single evaluation site, handed off by the same
at-most-once call and parked in the same triage lanes — deliberately not a
second mechanism beside the queue.

The tick gains a fourth job, `adopt`: label mechanics over the marked
issues, forming no judgment about who marked one. It consumes the mark and
every `claude-model:*` beside it, which is the whole exactly-once guard,
and it keeps one issue to one live item — a live prior run leaves the mark
waiting, a parked one is superseded.

The engine ships one task of its own, `engine/implement-request`, so a
request is an ordinary run rather than an item shape every downstream guard
has to except. It declares no code-work at all: the authorization a worker
would have performed is the precondition's.

The precondition IS the security check, at pickup. It refuses a request
nobody with push access asked for — push read from the permission API, not
from the payload's association, which is broader than the ask — and refuses
one withdrawn or gone. A read that could not answer is NOT a refusal: it
fails the run into the failure lane, open and re-queueable, because a
decline's write-back cannot reach an issue it cannot read.

Two contract additions: the precondition takes the occurrence as a third
argument, and `{ error }` joins go/no-go as the verdict a precondition
gives when it cannot answer. `model_from_request` is fenced to the built-in
task, which no pack can be.

Refs #1010

* Request mode: the design's amendment, the built-in id, and the vendor set

Three loose ends of the same change.

The design says the precondition reads the permission API; what it actually
reads is a `request` SIGNAL that made those reads — because a precondition
is pure over collected signals, and handing every pack's precondition a
GitHub client to give this one task two reads would widen far more than the
gate it guards. §16.4 says so, and says which half still holds the verdict.

The built-in task spells its own id literally: the declaration-shape check
parses task.mjs statically and cannot resolve the constant beside it. The
two are pinned together from the test.

And the engine's blanket "an engine .md is maintainer reference" vendor rule
was dropping the built-in task's task.md — a mount whose request session has
nothing to read. Whitelisted by pattern rather than by name, since the next
built-in task would otherwise be dropped silently, and the regression test
now WALKS the queue engine instead of listing its top level, which is what
let this through.

Refs #1010

* Rebase onto the terminal decoder main already landed

#1068 landed `outcomeOf` in the queue's own module — every spelling to a
canonical word, decoded in one place — which is the read half this branch
had written for itself. Its decoder is deleted in favour of that one, and
the dashboard sweep with it: main's already reads both vocabularies.

What is left here is the half nothing else did: the engine WRITES the
current spellings, the origin marker is neither written nor ensured, and
standing-versus-ad-hoc is derived from the item and the declaration.

Refs #1064

* Rebase onto #1071 and bump the growth pack for the contract prose

{"id":32368766036,"name":"Claudinite scheduler","display_title":"Claudinite scheduler","workflow_id":320696051,"run_number":403,"run_attempt":1,"event":"workflow_dispatch","status":"in_progress","head_branch":"main","head_sha":"208a0a5a705e8252b98e0de4f9892a7c1a01501c","head_commit":{"message":"The work-as-work engine catch-up: every #883 box (#1089)

* Executor: one run performs one item, and chains the rest

DESIGN §15.22 settled this on 2026-08-15 — "An executor performs a task.
It's not a current value. It's the essence of it." — and the engine kept
the pre-review loop. The `maxItems` surface deletes: a run claims one item,
sees it to its settle, and ends.

What carries the queue instead is the chain (§10): a run that settled its
item re-dispatches the executor workflow when anything is still pickable,
and the workflow gains a failure-continuation job so a run that DIES before
reaching that dispatch stalls the queue by a minute rather than an hour.

Pick order randomizes with it (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the
ready, so no unlucky head dominates a chain of one-item runs.

Refs #883

* Pin the executor's run shape: one item, a random head, a checked dispatch

The tests that pinned the pre-review contract went with it — `the loop stops
at maxItems` asserted the thing that is no longer true. What replaces it
asserts the structure: three pickable items of DIFFERENT titles (so the
same-title mutex is not what stops the run) and one settled; a chain that
continues only after a settle, and stands down after a lost race; and the
dispatch judged by status, since a 403 returns a body that reads fine.

Pick order gets a property test rather than a fixed order — a pinned order
would pass against a comparator that never shuffles.

Refs #883

* The terminal transition is code, and a close releases what it held

Two boxes of the work-as-work catch-up, which share a moment: the instant an
item closes.

The durable record (§15.18): the terminal comment now carries the
claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate
is shared with the tick's own job 2 rather than restated.

And converge-item.mjs (#892): a session ends by supplying the judgment —
which outcome, and the prose — while the code performs the five ordered side
effects. Both live agentic runs got part of that transition wrong from
prose, silently and differently.

Refs #883, Refs #892

* Pin the executor's own record and release paths (Refs #883)

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

Refs #883, Refs #924

* Design: the drain dispatches, and a dead chain escalates (Refs #883)

{"total_count":6,"workflow_runs":[{"id":32368841232,"name":"Claudinite executor","display_title":"Claudinite executor","workflow_id":335151064,"run_number":70,"run_attempt":1,"event":"workflow_dispatch","status":"in_progress","head_branch":"main","head_sha":"208a0a5a705e8252b98e0de4f9892a7c1a01501c","head_commit":{"message":"The work-as-work engine catch-up: every #883 box (#1089)

* Executor: one run performs one item, and chains the rest

DESIGN §15.22 settled this on 2026-08-15 — "An executor performs a task.
It's not a current value. It's the essence of it." — and the engine kept
the pre-review loop. The `maxItems` surface deletes: a run claims one item,
sees it to its settle, and ends.

What carries the queue instead is the chain (§10): a run that settled its
item re-dispatches the executor workflow when anything is still pickable,
and the workflow gains a failure-continuation job so a run that DIES before
reaching that dispatch stalls the queue by a minute rather than an hour.

Pick order randomizes with it (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the
ready, so no unlucky head dominates a chain of one-item runs.

Refs #883

* Pin the executor's run shape: one item, a random head, a checked dispatch

The tests that pinned the pre-review contract went with it — `the loop stops
at maxItems` asserted the thing that is no longer true. What replaces it
asserts the structure: three pickable items of DIFFERENT titles (so the
same-title mutex is not what stops the run) and one settled; a chain that
continues only after a settle, and stands down after a lost race; and the
dispatch judged by status, since a 403 returns a body that reads fine.

Pick order gets a property test rather than a fixed order — a pinned order
would pass against a comparator that never shuffles.

Refs #883

* The terminal transition is code, and a close releases what it held

Two boxes of the work-as-work catch-up, which share a moment: the instant an
item closes.

The durable record (§15.18): the terminal comment now carries the
claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate
is shared with the tick's own job 2 rather than restated.

And converge-item.mjs (#892): a session ends by supplying the judgment —
which outcome, and the prose — while the code performs the five ordered side
effects. Both live agentic runs got part of that transition wrong from
prose, silently and differently.

Refs #883, Refs #892

* Pin the executor's own record and release paths (Refs #883)

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

Refs #883, Refs #924

* Design: the drain dispatches, and a dead chain escalates (Refs #883)

* basics: a change proven only in production files its own verification

The loop that proves a change works stopped at the merge: anything whose
effect appears elsewhere — a pack reaching a member, a deploy, a rule the
next session loads — got verified when someone thought to ask.

The skill runs at the end of every change, beside the conversation capture,
and mostly files nothing: a change watched working, or pinned by a test that
ran, is already proven. Where it isn't, it files an issue naming the artifact
that says the change is live and the assertion that proves it works there.
The task reads that queue daily, stays silent while nothing is live, and
either proves the change or files what it found instead.

Closes #1091

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GHvPmJWFxPJ2TGVu3X2M47

* verify-in-production rides the request lane, not a task of its own

The queue is already the delayed-execution mechanism for ad-hoc work: a
marked issue is adopted, waits on Blocked-by, and a consumed mark means
re-marking re-adopts — the whole retry loop in existing vocabulary. The
standing daily task was a second queue beside it, keyed on a title prefix.

Dropped. The skill now files a deferred request (claude-task, Blocked-by
the PR, Not-before just past the expected release) whose brief tells the
run to verify when live, re-arm by bumping its own Not-before and re-mark
when not, and give up at a stated date. One generic gap closed in the
engine: adoption now carries a still-future Not-before: from the marked
issue onto the item, symmetric with Blocked-by — without it a re-marked
verification is picked within the hour, forever.

Refs #1091

* verify-in-production: automatic end to end, and the run decides nothing

Owner review: the verification is an unattended check by construction —
Verify: must be a read a run can make, a person only where no automatic
check can exist. A failure reopens the change's own issue (Original-issue:)
rather than filing a new one. The give-up marker is dropped, and the re-arm
extension is the filer's Retry-every: — the run just executes its playbook.

exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so

watermark nobody can see.

backwards.

the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions

tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

{"total_count":6,"workflow_runs":[{"id":32368841232,"name":"Claudinite executor","display_title":"Claudinite executor","workflow_id":335151064,"run_number":70,"run_attempt":1,"event":"workflow_dispatch","status":"in_progress","head_branch":"main","head_sha":"208a0a5a705e8252b98e0de4f9892a7c1a01501c","head_commit":{"message":"The work-as-work engine catch-up: every #883 box (#1089)

* Executor: one run performs one item, and chains the rest

DESIGN §15.22 settled this on 2026-08-15 — "An executor performs a task.
It's not a current value. It's the essence of it." — and the engine kept
the pre-review loop. The `maxItems` surface deletes: a run claims one item,
sees it to its settle, and ends.

What carries the queue instead is the chain (§10): a run that settled its
item re-dispatches the executor workflow when anything is still pickable,
and the workflow gains a failure-continuation job so a run that DIES before
reaching that dispatch stalls the queue by a minute rather than an hour.

Pick order randomizes with it (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the
ready, so no unlucky head dominates a chain of one-item runs.

Refs #883

* Pin the executor's run shape: one item, a random head, a checked dispatch

The tests that pinned the pre-review contract went with it — `the loop stops
at maxItems` asserted the thing that is no longer true. What replaces it
asserts the structure: three pickable items of DIFFERENT titles (so the
same-title mutex is not what stops the run) and one settled; a chain that
continues only after a settle, and stands down after a lost race; and the
dispatch judged by status, since a 403 returns a body that reads fine.

Pick order gets a property test rather than a fixed order — a pinned order
would pass against a comparator that never shuffles.

Refs #883

* The terminal transition is code, and a close releases what it held

Two boxes of the work-as-work catch-up, which share a moment: the instant an
item closes.

The durable record (§15.18): the terminal comment now carries the
claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate
is shared with the tick's own job 2 rather than restated.

And converge-item.mjs (#892): a session ends by supplying the judgment —
which outcome, and the prose — while the code performs the five ordered side
effects. Both live agentic runs got part of that transition wrong from
prose, silently and differently.

Refs #883, Refs #892

* Pin the executor's own record and release paths (Refs #883)

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

Refs #883, Refs #924

* Design: the drain dispatches, and a dead chain escalates (Refs #883)

---------

* basics: a change proven only in production files its own verification

The loop that proves a change works stopped at the merge: anything whose
effect appears elsewhere — a pack reaching a member, a deploy, a rule the
next session loads — got verified when someone thought to ask.

The skill runs at the end of every change, beside the conversation capture,
and mostly files nothing: a change watched working, or pinned by a test that
ran, is already proven. Where it isn't, it files an issue naming the artifact
that says the change is live and the assertion that proves it works there.
The task reads that queue daily, stays silent while nothing is live, and
either proves the change or files what it found instead.

Closes #1091

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GHvPmJWFxPJ2TGVu3X2M47

* verify-in-production rides the request lane, not a task of its own

The queue is already the delayed-execution mechanism for ad-hoc work: a
marked issue is adopted, waits on Blocked-by, and a consumed mark means
re-marking re-adopts — the whole retry loop in existing vocabulary. The
standing daily task was a second queue beside it, keyed on a title prefix.

Dropped. The skill now files a deferred request (claude-task, Blocked-by
the PR, Not-before just past the expected release) whose brief tells the
run to verify when live, re-arm by bumping its own Not-before and re-mark
when not, and give up at a stated date. One generic gap closed in the
engine: adoption now carries a still-future Not-before: from the marked
issue onto the item, symmetric with Blocked-by — without it a re-marked
verification is picked within the hour, forever.

Refs #1091

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GHvPmJWFxPJ2TGVu3X2M47

* merge-to-main: a recipe, not an explanation

Refs #1091

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GHvPmJWFxPJ2TGVu3X2M47

* verify-in-production: automatic end to end, and the run decides nothing

Owner review: the verification is an unattended check by construction —
Verify: must be a read a run can make, a person only where no automatic
check can exist. A failure reopens the change's own issue (Original-issue:)
rather than filing a new one. The give-up marker is dropped, and the re-arm
extension is the filer's Retry-every: — the run just executes its playbook.

Refs #1091

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GHvPmJWFxPJ2TGVu3X2M47

content.text: The main-branch run settled exactly one item and correctly did **not** re-dispatch (nothing else pickable — #1097 is blocked until tomorrow). Now checking my janitor wake, which produced no item:

{"total_count":8,"workflow_runs":[{"id":32368932530,"name":"Claudinite scheduler","display_title":"Claudinite scheduler","workflow_id":320696051,"run_number":404,"run_attempt":1,"event":"workflow_dispatch","status":"completed","conclusion":"success","head_branch":"main","head_sha":"208a0a5a705e8252b98e0de4f9892a7c1a01501c","head_commit":{"message":"The work-as-work engine catch-up: every #883 box (#1089)

* Executor: one run performs one item, and chains the rest

DESIGN §15.22 settled this on 2026-08-15 — "An executor performs a task.
It's not a current value. It's the essence of it." — and the engine kept
the pre-review loop. The `maxItems` surface deletes: a run claims one item,
sees it to its settle, and ends.

What carries the queue instead is the chain (§10): a run that settled its
item re-dispatches the executor workflow when anything is still pickable,
and the workflow gains a failure-continuation job so a run that DIES before
reaching that dispatch stalls the queue by a minute rather than an hour.

Pick order randomizes with it (§15.20): urgent first, then random among the
ready, so no unlucky head dominates a chain of one-item runs.

Refs #883

* Pin the executor's run shape: one item, a random head, a checked dispatch

The tests that pinned the pre-review contract went with it — `the loop stops
at maxItems` asserted the thing that is no longer true. What replaces it
asserts the structure: three pickable items of DIFFERENT titles (so the
same-title mutex is not what stops the run) and one settled; a chain that
continues only after a settle, and stands down after a lost race; and the
dispatch judged by status, since a 403 returns a body that reads fine.

Pick order gets a property test rather than a fixed order — a pinned order
would pass against a comparator that never shuffles.

Refs #883

* The terminal transition is code, and a close releases what it held

Two boxes of the work-as-work catch-up, which share a moment: the instant an
item closes.

The durable record (§15.18): the terminal comment now carries the
claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate
is shared with the tick's own job 2 rather than restated.

And converge-item.mjs (#892): a session ends by supplying the judgment —
which outcome, and the prose — while the code performs the five ordered side
effects. Both live agentic runs got part of that transition wrong from
prose, silently and differently.

Refs #883, Refs #892

* Pin the executor's own record and release paths (Refs #883)

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction

* Queue labels: task:done/task:obsolete, and the origin marker retired

DESIGN §15.25/§15.26 renamed the terminal labels and deleted the origin
marker; the fielded engine still wrote the old vocabulary. This is the
engine-side half.

The terminals are `task:done` and `task:obsolete`, one namespace with the
state labels. Labels are stored data on closed issues fleet-wide, so the
read side accepts every retired spelling and maps it STRAIGHT to today's
in one pass: `terminalOfLabels` is the one decoder, and the old constants
stay exported so a fielded pack that imports them still loads.

Standing versus ad-hoc is now derived rather than marked: the standing
item is the one titled with the task and nothing else, whose task is on a
calendar; a `manual` task's item and every qualified one are ad-hoc. The
occurrence guard, the dedupe, the `after` yield and the roll-vs-close
decision all read that instead of `origin:schedule`, which is no longer
written or ensured — only tolerated on items an older engine filed.

One behaviour follows from the derivation: an unqualified hand-created
item for a scheduled task WOULD be that task's standing item, so
`create-work-item` refuses it and names the two levers that do what the
operator meant (`--wake`, `--qualifier`).

The dashboard reads terminals through the engine decoder, and folds a
cached summary's legacy KEYS the same way — otherwise those rows land on
a key nothing initialised.

Refs #1064

* Ad-hoc requests: a marked issue becomes an ordinary queue run

Mark an issue `claude-task` and the next tick queues a run for it. The mode
is dispatched by the same tick, claimed under the same lease, judged by a
precondition at the same single evaluation site, handed off by the same
at-most-once call and parked in the same triage lanes — deliberately not a
second mechanism beside the queue.

The tick gains a fourth job, `adopt`: label mechanics over the marked
issues, forming no judgment about who marked one. It consumes the mark and
every `claude-model:*` beside it, which is the whole exactly-once guard,
and it keeps one issue to one live item — a live prior run leaves the mark
waiting, a parked one is superseded.

The engine ships one task of its own, `engine/implement-request`, so a
request is an ordinary run rather than an item shape every downstream guard
has to except. It declares no code-work at all: the authorization a worker
would have performed is the precondition's.

The precondition IS the security check, at pickup. It refuses a request
nobody with push access asked for — push read from the permission API, not
from the payload's association, which is broader than the ask — and refuses
one withdrawn or gone. A read that could not answer is NOT a refusal: it
fails the run into the failure lane, open and re-queueable, because a
decline's write-back cannot reach an issue it cannot read.

Two contract additions: the precondition takes the occurrence as a third
argument, and `{ error }` joins go/no-go as the verdict a precondition
gives when it cannot answer. `model_from_request` is fenced to the built-in
task, which no pack can be.

Refs #1010

* Request mode: the design's amendment, the built-in id, and the vendor set

Three loose ends of the same change.

The design says the precondition reads the permission API; what it actually
reads is a `request` SIGNAL that made those reads — because a precondition
is pure over collected signals, and handing every pack's precondition a
GitHub client to give this one task two reads would widen far more than the
gate it guards. §16.4 says so, and says which half still holds the verdict.

The built-in task spells its own id literally: the declaration-shape check
parses task.mjs statically and cannot resolve the constant beside it. The
two are pinned together from the test.

And the engine's blanket "an engine .md is maintainer reference" vendor rule
was dropping the built-in task's task.md — a mount whose request session has
nothing to read. Whitelisted by pattern rather than by name, since the next
built-in task would otherwise be dropped silently, and the regression test
now WALKS the queue engine instead of listing its top level, which is what
let this through.

Refs #1010

* Rebase onto the terminal decoder main already landed

#1068 landed `outcomeOf` in the queue's own module — every spelling to a
canonical word, decoded in one place — which is the read half this branch
had written for itself. Its decoder is deleted in favour of that one, and
the dashboard sweep with it: main's already reads both vocabularies.

What is left here is the half nothing else did: the engine WRITES the
current spellings, the origin marker is neither written nor ensured, and
standing-versus-ad-hoc is derived from the item and the declaration.

Refs #1064

* Rebase onto #1071 and bump the growth pack for the contract prose

Refs #1010

claudinite-task-exec line, because Actions logs expire and for an agentless
run the item is the only trace there will ever be. Where the record
vocabulary has no true answer — an approval park is a run that SUCCEEDED and
left a PR — it writes none rather than inventing a fifth status every
decoder in the fleet would have to learn.

The readiness re-check at close (§15.19): whoever closes an item releases
the dependents it was holding, so a chain link runs in seconds rather than
waiting out the hour. The tick stays the backstop for every close this code
never performs — a human's, or a session that stopped early. The predicate
is shared with the tick's own job 2 rather than restated.

which outcome, and the prose — while the code performs the five ordered side
effects. Both live agentic runs got part of that transition wrong from
prose, silently and differently.

Refs #883, Refs #892

* Pin the executor's own record and release paths (Refs #883)

* The heartbeat, the hold, and the two bounds they retire

The heartbeat (§15.15): the executor comments on its own item every 15
minutes while the work step runs, so long work is legal rather than dark.
With it, the tick's reclaim stops measuring the ISSUE's silence and measures
the HOLDER's — its last live claim or heartbeat — which is #924: any comment
moved `updated_at`, including the one an executor that lost the claim race
writes on its way out, so the reclaim of an item nobody held kept deferring.
A struck claim is not a sign of life.

Two rationales the heartbeat invalidates are rewritten rather than left
standing: the run cap that used to bound a work step (leases.mjs), and
code-work's claim that overlap with a zombie is excluded by construction
(code-work-run.mjs) — it no longer is, and re-entrancy is what covers it,
which is why the contract asks for re-entrancy and not idempotency.

The tick/drain decoupling (§15.16): the drain job dispatches the executor
workflow instead of being one, so it leaves the tick's concurrency group. It
therefore runs no task code, which is why the tick stub's secrets marker
goes — and why `withDeclaredSecrets` now stamps at the marker or not at all.
Its old fallback would have stamped every task secret into the one job the
design says must never hold one.

The operator hold (§15.24): one repo variable, stamped into all four
workflows, checked as the first act of both entry points — before the config
load, before the first API call. It gates STARTS, not running work.

A dead chain now escalates: after three consecutive deaths the continuation
stops re-dispatching and says so on the workflow-failure issue, because a
queue that has quietly stopped draining is the one failure where every
individual run looks like an ordinary death.

Refs #883, Refs #924

* Design: the drain dispatches, and a dead chain escalates (Refs #883)
